title: The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand: Project Meridian FX APAC
body:
The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand: Project Meridian FX APAC | Bank of England – the UK's central bank Our use of cookies We use necessary cookies to make our site work. We’d also like to use some non-essential cookies (including third-party cookies) to help us improve the site. By clicking ‘Accept recommended settings’ on this banner, you accept our use of analytics cookies.   For more information on how these cookies work please see our Cookie policy . Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand: Project Meridian FX APAC Joint media release Published on  
        13 November 2026 News Release The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand today published the findings from their collaboration on foreign exchange (FX) settlement under Project Meridian FX APAC. footnote [1] The project showed that synchronisation – a service that coordinates movements of central bank money – could be one approach to supporting interoperability across wholesale settlement environments built on different technologies and operating models. This marks significant progress in making cross-border FX transactions safer and more efficient, and supporting interoperability as different forms of money evolve in different ways. In light of the Bank of England’s plans to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028, footnote [2] the findings provide valuable insight into how the approach could be developed into a live service. Building on the earlier work, footnote [3] Project Meridian FX APAC tested payment-versus-payment FX settlement footnote [4] and multilateral net FX across the three central banks’ test environments, spanning both Real-Time Gross Settlement and Distributed Ledger Technology-based settlement systems. The project encompassed a wider range of currencies, technologies, infrastructures and time zones. Partior, the project’s delivery partner, developed, integrated and tested the Synchronisation Operator footnote [5] prototype for the trial. The trial demonstrated that synchronised settlement can be achieved across central bank systems with different technologies and capabilities, while identifying the requirements and trade-offs involved. They also demonstrated how multilateral net FX settlement can support banks in using their liquidity more efficiently by netting payments against each other. The project also examined the legal, regulatory and oversight considerations for applying synchronised FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. The analysis was informed by perspectives from the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, who participated as observer central banks. The project’s findings and insights are published across three complementary reports: Introduction and Executive Summary , Technical Report , and Policy Report . Together, they set out the experimental results, key technical findings and policy considerations. These results provide insights for further exploration of synchronisation as a means of enabling safer and more efficient FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. Future work could involve extending the existing approach to additional jurisdictions and industry participants, a wider range of currencies and transaction scenarios, and further consider the legal arrangements needed in practice. Tom Mutton, Executive Director of Payments, Innovation and Fintech at the Bank of England, said, ‘Innovation has the greatest impact when it addresses real world challenges. Project Meridian FX APAC provides practical evidence of how synchronised settlement could help reduce risk and improve efficiency in cross-border FX transactions. The results provide a strong foundation for further collaboration as we explore how this approach could be developed towards real-world use’. Kenneth Gay, Chief FinTech Officer at the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said, ‘Cross-border settlement increasingly takes place across systems built on different technologies and operating models. Project Meridian FX APAC has shown how synchronisation could help enable PvP settlement across these diverse environments, reducing settlement risk while supporting greater interoperability’. Pucktada Treeratpituk, Director of Payment Systems and Financial Technology Policy Department at the Bank of Thailand, said, ‘Project Meridian FX APAC successfully demonstrated that synchronisation can work across diverse wholesale settlement systems, making cross-border FX safer and more efficient while preserving trust in central bank money. The insights on technical integration, operating models and regulatory considerations established a practical foundation for modernising wholesale settlement infrastructure’. About the Bank of England The Bank of England, established in 1694, is the central bank of the United Kingdom. It is responsible for maintaining monetary and financial stability. In this capacity, the Bank of England undertakes a range of functions, including the implementation of monetary policy, oversight of payment systems, prudential regulation of financial institutions, and the issuance of currency. The Bank of England also plays a key role in safeguarding financial stability through its work on systemic risk, resolution frameworks, and market operations. In relation to UK payments, the Bank of England performs a number of operational functions, including acting as the operator of the UK’s Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system and the CHAPS payment system. About the Monetary Authority of Singapore The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is Singapore’s central bank and integrated financial regulator. As a central bank, MAS promotes sustained, non-inflationary economic growth through the conduct of monetary policy and close macroeconomic surveillance and analysis. It manages Singapore’s exchange rate, official foreign reserves, and liquidity in the banking sector. As an integrated financial supervisor, MAS fosters a sound financial services sector through its prudential oversight of all financial institutions in Singapore – banks, insurers, capital market intermediaries, financial advisors and financial market infrastructure. It is also responsible for well-functioning financial markets, sound conduct, and investor education. MAS also works with the financial industry to foster the growth of Singapore as an international financial centre. About the Bank of Thailand The Bank of Thailand (BOT) is the central bank and regulator of financial services in Thailand. The BOT is responsible for maintaining monetary stability, financial institution system stability and payment systems stability. In relation to Thailand payments, the BOT functions as the operator of the Bank of Thailand Automated High-value Transfer Network (BAHTNET), which constitutes a core financial infrastructure facilitating high-value funds transfer on a RTGS basis. For media queries, please contact: Bank of England Press Enquiries Tel: 020 3461 4411 Email: press@bankofengland.co.uk Monetary Authority of Singapore Hidayah Rahim Deputy Director (Communications) Tel.: +65 64225609 Email: hidayah_rahim@mas.gov.sg Bank of Thailand Payment Systems and Financial Technology Policy Department Tel: +66 356 7077 Email: FinTechDept@bot.or.th This project, to explore the technical and policy implications of settling foreign exchange (FX) transactions using synchronised settlement mechanisms, was announced in November 2025 . The Bank of England announced their intention to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028, as part of their Call for Input on the Future of Tokenisation with the FCA. For further information on the Bank of England’s synchronisation plans, see Synchronisation | Bank of England – the UK's central bank . Project Meridian FX, led by the BIS Innovation Hub London in collaboration with the Bank of England, Bank of France, Deutsche Bundesbank, Bank of Italy and European Central Bank, tested synchronisation as a solution to cross-border interoperability. Refer to Project Meridian FX: exploring synchronised settlement in FX for more information. PvP settlement reduces FX settlement risk by ensuring that the transfer of one currency occurs if and only if the transfer of the other currency also occurs. According to the 2025 BIS Triennial Central Bank Survey , more than US$1.4 trillion, or 10%, of average daily FX settlement in April 2025 remained fully exposed to settlement risk. A Synchronisation Operator is a coordination layer that enables atomic settlement across different settlement systems by ensuring that linked transfers occur together, or not at all. title: Isabel Schnabel: Made in Europe
body:
Made in Europe Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Isabel Schnabel Member of the ECB's Executive Board SPEECH Made in Europe Speech by Isabel Schnabel, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Economics Conference, Bank of Lithuania Vilnius, 13 November 2026 We are living through a period of radical transformation. Technological progress is accelerating alongside profound geopolitical shifts, rewriting the rules that have governed global growth, trade and security for decades. [ 1 ] In this polarised world, Europe is often portrayed as a continent in decline, squeezed between geopolitical rivals, held back by excessive regulation and struggling to keep pace with rapid technological change. In my remarks this morning, I will argue that although this narrative is appealing in its simplicity, it is misleading. By many measures, Europe is among the regions with the highest quality of life, grounded in strong institutions, a high degree of social protection and an exceptional capacity to adapt in times of crisis. Europe can build on these fundamentals to become even stronger. I will explain that the key is to unlock the full potential of the Single Market – one of Europe’s most powerful assets – to deliver what Europe lacks today: not talent, not ideas, not research – but scale. A 28th regime would be a true game changer in this respect. By giving firms seamless access to the entire European market, it would provide the scale needed to convert innovation into economic growth. It would allow Europe to compete as one economy rather than 27, and help create something Europe has long been missing: a true “Made in Europe” brand. Europe leading the way in quality of life and democratic values Europe stands out globally for its quality of life, built on strong economic, social and institutional foundations. Happiness and life satisfaction in Europe consistently rank among the highest in the world (Slide 2). This goes beyond income or wealth – it reflects the broader conditions that allow people to live secure, fulfilling and prosperous lives. Social protection, accessible public infrastructure, high-quality public education and family support help turn economic prosperity into tangible improvements in people’s lives. [ 2 ] Health outcomes are particularly revealing here. A child born in Spain or Italy can expect to live five years longer than a child born in the United States (Slide 3), despite the United States spending a far larger share of GDP on healthcare than any other advanced economy. Even among the wealthiest Americans, mortality rates are merely at the level of the poorest populations in parts of Europe. [ 3 ] Europeans also benefit from strong institutions. A growing share of the world’s population now lives under de facto autocratic rule, while attacks on democratic freedoms continue at an alarming pace (Slide 4). Against this backdrop, Europe’s continued commitment to democracy, the rule of law and institutional checks and balances underpin trust and policy credibility, while independent media ensure accountability and transparency. These institutions and principles give people confidence in their future and in the fairness of society, even in the face of adversity. Rethinking the transatlantic prosperity gap: more leisure time, greater equality So, throughout its history, Europe has made deliberate choices about the kind of society it wants to be. But while these choices have resulted in better life outcomes, they have also weighed on GDP per capita, adjusted for the cost of living, which is one of the most used indicators of economic prosperity. By this measure, the euro area ranks below other advanced economies (Slide 5). [ 4 ] Part of this difference reflects the fact that some euro area economies are still catching up, mainly in eastern Europe. These countries are mostly growing rapidly, but their incomes remain below the euro area average, which dampens the headline number. Yet, a substantial gap remains even for the more advanced euro area economies. Interpreting this gap requires careful analysis along three dimensions. [ 5 ] First, a large part of the gap in income levels reflects less work rather than less productive work. On average, an employee in the United States works around 40 days more per year than an employee in the euro area (Slide 6, left-hand side). [ 6 ] A simple counterfactual shows that if Europeans were to work as many hours as Americans, holding productivity per hour and the employment rate constant, euro area real GDP per capita would be 21% higher. [ 7 ] That would close about two-thirds of the current real income gap with the United States (Slide 6, right-hand side). [ 8 ] So, part of the observed difference in relative income levels reflects preferences and institutions rather than low productivity. Shorter working weeks, more generous vacation entitlements and a higher prevalence of part-time employment in Europe are the result of institutional, social and personal choices. Second, growth in Europe is more inclusive. Real GDP per capita is an average across regions, individuals and sectors, which means that very high incomes at the top of the distribution can pull the mean upwards. In the United States, the top 10% of earners today account for around 37% of national income after taxes, a considerable rise since 1980 (Slide 7, left-hand side). [ 9 ] In the euro area the share is significantly lower, around 27% on average. So, in the United States, a large share of income does not accrue to 90% of the population. The typical American lives in a USD 45,000 economy, not a USD 67,000 one. [ 10 ] This difference also reflects that recent income gains are increasingly concentrated in certain sectors and regions. Since 2000, more than a quarter of total growth in value added per employee in the United States has accrued in the information and communications technology sector – an industry that accounts for less than 2% of total employment (Slide 7, right-hand side). As the exceptional expansion of large technology companies has been concentrated in a small number of US states, the growth performance of the typical state has been more modest, even as aggregate US GDP per capita has surged. Indeed, growth in real GDP per capita in the median US state and that in the median euro area country have evolved largely in lockstep (Slide 8). Standard GDP per capita comparisons thus overstate the disparity in living standards between the United States and the euro area. Europeans work fewer hours, enjoy stronger social protection and live in more equal societies. But to protect these advantages, Europe needs sustained growth. And this growth is threatened by persistently weak productivity growth in the euro area – the third dimension. Over the past three decades, output per hour worked has risen more slowly than in several peer economies, reflecting less capital deepening, smaller firms and the lack of diffusion of new technologies (Slide 9). [ 11 ] This divergence in productivity growth has led to a gradual widening of GDP per capita gaps over time. As productivity growth is the key driver of sustainable improvements in living standards, closing this gap has rightly become a key policy priority in Europe. [ 12 ] The thriving South: from crisis economies to growth leaders The benefits of addressing structural headwinds are clearly visible in parts of the currency union. Take the south of the euro area. A decade ago, this region was synonymous with crises, austerity and soaring unemployment. Today, those countries are among the fastest-growing economies in Europe (Slide 10, left-hand side). They have been attracting record levels of investment (Slide 10, right-hand side), unemployment has been declining at an impressive pace (Slide 11, left-hand side) and financing conditions relative to Germany, despite some recent spread widening, remain close to their most favourable levels since the global financial crisis of 2008, reflecting economic convergence and financial integration (Slide 11, right-hand side). As a result, these economies have been able to create space to reduce deficits without undermining the recovery, thereby supporting fiscal consolidation and improving debt sustainability (Slide 12, left-hand side). To a large extent, the momentum in the southern periphery reflects a sustained improvement in underlying economic capacity. According to the European Commission, potential growth in Spain, Portugal and Greece is projected to be measurably higher than the euro area average in the years to come (Slide 12, right-hand side). Spain, for example, has emerged as a European leader in renewable energy. This has significantly reduced wholesale electricity prices and the country’s vulnerability to global energy price shocks, transforming it into a European hub for the energy-intensive industries of the future. [ 13 ] Ireland, meanwhile, has become a global hotspot for technology, pharmaceutical and life science companies. It is one of the most efficient countries in which to do business and it has the highest share of tertiary students in natural sciences, mathematics and statistics fields in the EU. This transformation is the outcome of political choices and social resilience. These economies had to endure painful adjustments when structural change was unfolding, and the population was willing to embrace these changes. This is partly also a European success story. Through instruments such as Next Generation EU, substantial common resources were mobilised to support investment, accelerate reforms and strengthen growth potential in countries that had limited fiscal space to overcome the COVID-19 pandemic. Stagnating Germany: export-driven business model no longer viable in a fragmenting world So, the narrative that Europe is underperforming does not hold up in large parts of the currency union. Today, economic headwinds are felt most acutely in the euro area’s traditional core, albeit for different reasons. In France, efforts to reduce the fiscal deficit have stalled due to political resistance. Sustained consolidation will depend on striking a careful balance between reduced spending and growth-enhancing policies, a task which will require difficult political compromises. Some northern European countries have struggled to regain momentum after the pandemic. Austria, for example, was in recession both in 2023 and 2024 and grew only moderately in 2025. Most attention has, however, focused on Germany, which has been navigating an extended period of subdued growth. From 2019 to 2024, its real GDP per capita fell by 0.5%. The headwinds are numerous. Demographic change is increasingly weighing on potential growth and thus on the sustainability of social security systems (Slide 13, left-hand side). Energy costs remain elevated compared with pre-pandemic levels. And protectionism as well as global competition, especially from China, are hitting Germany particularly hard (Slide 13, right-hand side). As export growth has softened, Germany’s economic weakness is often attributed to a deterioration in competitiveness. While this has played a role, treating eroding export market shares as the main cause of stagnation is a misdiagnosis of the problem. In fact, Germany’s export performance neither dramatically outpaced its peers before the pandemic, nor has it materially lagged behind since (Slide 14, left-hand side). [ 14 ] Over the past ten years, Germany’s real goods exports have broadly tracked the global cycle. Germany also did not boast particularly high growth when it ran massive trade surpluses. On average between 1999 and 2019, it grew by just 1.4% annually, less than most other advanced economies (Slide 14, right-hand side). The key shortfall, therefore, is not a collapse in external demand or a unique deterioration in competitiveness. [ 15 ] Rather, it is a sustained weakness in domestic demand that makes Germany’s economy more prone than others to crises abroad. Especially in a more fragmented world, its export-driven business model is no longer viable. Since 1999, real private consumption in Germany has grown by less than 1% per year on average, significantly less than in most other advanced economies, as the reforms implemented in the early 2000s intentionally suppressed real wage growth (Slide 15, left-hand side). These policies reduced the labour share and increased corporate profits and savings, mirrored in the sharp rise in Germany’s current account surplus (Slide 15, right-hand side). [ 16 ] As domestic investment remained subdued, these savings were essentially exported, financing growth elsewhere. [ 17 ] If German households and firms had consumed and invested more over the past two decades, the trade surplus would have been lower, but GDP growth would likely have been stronger and more balanced. Even today, Germany’s current account surplus continues to significantly exceed the level suggested by economic fundamentals. Estimates by the European Commission suggest that Germany would be expected to post a current account surplus of about 1.2% of its GDP – a fraction of the current level. [ 18 ] Wise fiscal spending and structural reforms can boost potential growth Germany has taken steps to address this macroeconomic imbalance and the decline in potential growth. Fiscal policy is one key instrument. The fiscal impulse that has taken shape is the largest since the Second World War and is a welcome step in the right direction. Targeted public investment in infrastructure, support for the green and digital transformations and measures that strengthen Germany’s defence capacity not only bolster domestic demand, but also enhance the supply side, thereby lifting the German economy out of stagnation. Higher public spending, if allocated wisely and accompanied by structural reforms, boosts potential growth and crowds in private investment. This channel is particularly important in Germany, where firms have historically responded to rising energy costs and excessive bureaucracy by expanding production abroad. This is reflected in Germany’s outward foreign direct investment position, which has increased strongly in recent years (Slide 16, left-hand side). In other words, the domestic investment gap is not due to a lack of profitable investment ideas among German companies; it is an allocation choice. Germany’s industrial know-how remains formidable, but its capital is highly mobile. The country’s “hidden champions” – specialised firms that dominate global niches – continue to innovate and expand. At the latest count, Germany still hosts nearly half of the world’s hidden champions, more than the United States, China and Japan combined (Slide 16, right-hand side). [ 19 ] With an ambitious reform agenda and a courageous investment initiative, Germany can anchor more private capital, innovation and growth within the country. And given its fiscal position, Germany can afford this response, especially if the measures help reverse the trend decline in potential growth. If they do, the additional spending will strengthen rather than weaken Germany’s fiscal sustainability, with positive spillover effects to the rest of Europe. Europe lacks scale, not ideas: the case for a 28th regime All in all, these points reinforce the broader message that the picture in Europe should be one of optimism – not because the challenges are small, but because Europe has the capacity and the tools to meet them. Europe has a vast reservoir of talent, ideas and research. In absolute terms, the EU produces more publications than the United States in every major subject area and is almost on a par with China (Slide 17). [ 20 ] Each year, Europe also generates more early-stage start-ups than the United States. Europe is not yet “losing” the AI race either. History shows that the bulk of productivity gains from past general-purpose technologies have come not from inventing them, but from adopting them widely across the economy. [ 21 ] Europe has several large sectors – such as manufacturing, energy, healthcare and public services – where AI adoption can deliver major productivity gains. Indeed, Europe’s productivity gap with the United States widened in the early 2000s not because Europe stopped innovating, but because it was slower to adopt information and communications technologies (ICT). [ 22 ] One key reason was that investment in ICT involves high fixed and organisational costs, which US firms – operating in a large, integrated market – were able to spread over a broader customer base. In the United States, firms with more than 250 employees account for almost 60% of total employment. In many euro area countries, this share is closer to 20%. In other words, Europe’s problem is a lack of scale. [ 23 ] Despite decades of integration, regulatory and administrative barriers still obstruct the free movement of services and goods through the Single Market. These internal barriers are estimated to be equivalent to tariffs of 96% for services and 67% for goods (Slide 18). [ 24 ] Some industries, such as food production and construction, face even greater hurdles. As a result, in the services sector, which accounts for some 75% of total gross value added, intra-EU trade is no higher than trade with non-EU countries. Many proposals on how to reduce these internal barriers are already on the table, ranging from deeper capital markets integration to a common European energy, defence and digital infrastructure. [ 25 ] The most powerful idea is the creation of a 28th regime: a unified European corporate framework open to firms of all sizes and sectors. For decades, the Single Market has been built primarily through harmonisation across the 27 national systems. In many areas, this approach has worked well. But in others, it has reached its limits, as we have seen with the proliferation of national gold-plating in the transposition of EU directives. In particular, business founders today still need to navigate a complex patchwork of legal systems, corporate codes and regulatory regimes. This fragmentation acts like an internal tariff wall, making it costly and difficult to expand across borders, especially into smaller countries, such as Lithuania. Thereby it discourages growth and ultimately slows innovation. The result is that too many European firms remain too small, while start-ups often choose to become American companies the moment they start to grow. A striking number incorporate not under European law but as Delaware corporations, often well before they have any meaningful presence in the United States. As a result, many unicorn companies in the United States have European founders. This is no accident. Incorporating a company in Delaware takes just a few days, or even hours, and comes with very low costs. The legal framework is standardised, predictable and immediately understandable to global investors. By contrast, scaling across Europe still requires legal reinvention country by country with costly notary procedures and fragmented firm registries. Moreover, while funding in Europe is relatively abundant at the founding stage, it is much more difficult to obtain in the growth and exit phases. Initial public offerings often yield unattractive pricing due to the lack of a liquid market, which encourages new European companies to look for funding elsewhere. The consequence is that, while Europe excels at generating ideas and building start-ups, it struggles to keep them in Europe as they grow. How a 28th regime can help boost innovation and productivity A 28th regime can change that. [ 26 ] The concept is simple: under a 28th regime, a company could choose to incorporate as a genuinely European firm, which the European Commission refers to as “EU Inc . ”. [ 27 ] That company would operate under a unified set of rules for core elements of company law, governance, shareholder rights and employee financial compensation. The incorporation process would be quick, cheap and fully digital. Participation would be voluntary, and the regime would be open to companies of all sizes, in all sectors. That openness matters. It is neither possible nor desirable to predict which technologies, firms or industries will drive Europe’s growth in the future. And it would be counterproductive to limit the regime to young firms, as its very purpose is to enable firms to grow and succeed. By offering firms a truly European corporate framework, the regime would lower barriers to cross-border activity, make it easier to raise capital and attract talent, and allow innovative companies to scale more quickly across the Union. To achieve this, the legal implementation is critical. Ideally, the 28th regime should be established through an EU regulation that is directly applicable across all member states, as foreseen in the current proposal. Otherwise, Europe risks ending up with 27 versions of the 28th regime, recreating the very fragmentation it seeks to eliminate. [ 28 ] A 28th regime would complement national systems, not replace them. It is not an attempt to harmonise labour law or social security systems – these would remain in national hands. Nor is the 28th regime a backdoor to tax harmonisation: corporate tax rates, tax bases and other aspects of fiscal policy would continue to be determined by Member States. [ 29 ] Its purpose is narrower in focus: to remove unnecessary legal fragmentation and uncertainty for firms that wish to expand across borders, and to make European companies as attractive to global venture capital, private equity and institutional investors as Delaware corporations are today. The 28th regime would thus help ensure that the next generation of European companies remains European, not just in terms of where ideas are created, but also where value is built. The proposal currently under discussion could be an important step in that direction. It would help boost innovation and, ultimately, productivity growth, which has long been Europe’s Achilles heel. Reigniting it is essential for sustaining prosperity in an ageing society and a fragmenting world. By contrast, should the current proposal be watered down, for example by leaving room for national gold-plating or limiting harmonisation in the area of insolvency, it would risk becoming another lost opportunity. Conclusion I want to conclude with a simple point: Europe is a continent with huge potential. Despite the challenges we face, it remains one of the most prosperous, innovative and socially cohesive regions in the world. Europe leads the way in quality of life, excels in scientific output and sets global standards in environmental protection. Europeans are bound together not only by treaties and regulations, but by shared values: multilateral cooperation and respect for democratic institutions and the rule of law. In a world increasingly drifting towards autocracy, Europe’s institutional integrity is a significant asset. It makes Europe one of the most attractive places in the world to live, work and invest, offering stability, predictability and opportunity to people and businesses from across the globe. Europe’s central challenge is not a lack of ideas or talent. It is a lack of scale. And Europe has the power to change that itself. The 28th regime offers a concrete and powerful way to address this problem – a framework that allows innovation to thrive, firms to scale and productivity to rise. By helping to build a truly frictionless Single Market, it can establish a “Made in Europe” brand for companies that stands for innovation, excellence and legal certainty. And that is the narrative that Europe needs to reclaim. Thank you. This speech is a slightly updated version of a speech delivered at a lecture in memory of Eugen Böhm von Bawerk at the Österreichische Akademie der Wissenschaften in Vienna on 11 February 2026. We are releasing five new tools in Google Flow to help you create professional visuals and stories. These tools allow you to design consistent characters, apply retro digital styles, simulate complex light effects, and improve your phone footage with cinematic camera angles. You can use these features to speed up your creative process, maintain a signature look, and bring your unique ideas to life. Try them out in our creative studio today. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today, we're releasing five new tools that show how you can keep pushing the boundaries of visual storytelling in Google Flow , our AI creative studio. These five tools — all built by creatives — prove there’s increasingly no limit to what you can build in Google Flow. See how they can help you shape your next story, from concept to final cut. 1. Character Poster , by artist and filmmaker James Gerde James Gerde treats his social feeds like curated galleries where visual consistency is everything. He built Character Poster to turn simple story concepts into polished, beautifully designed visuals. It helps creators maintain a signature style across their social stories — and can save hours of production work. A cinematic “let’s go to the beach” poster generated with Character Poster by James Gerde. 2. Character Arc , by filmmaker and visual storyteller Anurag Tiwari Anurag Tiwari built Character Arc to show how a character changes over time. It lets storytellers visualize the same character across different ages and life stages without losing their core look, speeding up character development before full production begins. For his documentary “Children of the Sun ,” which features present-day interviews with subjects reflecting on events from 1974, Anurag is using Character Arc to trace the protagonist’s life from childhood through adulthood. "It helps me build his background while keeping him recognizable as the same person across different periods of the story," Anurag says. A visual timeline of the protagonist generated with Character Arc for “Children of the Sun.” 3. Pixel Machine , also by Anurag Tiwari Inspired by his love for retro digital aesthetics, Anurag also created Pixel Machine to give filmmakers and artists a playground that goes beyond polished AI visuals. It converts images into bitmap, ASCII, CRT, pixel art, and glitch styles, making it easier to design stylized title treatments, transitions, and music video visuals. A stylized ASCII art animation and effects treatment, generated with Pixel Machine. 4. Lucid Glass , by artist and creative director Ezra Paulekas Ezra Paulekas designed Lucid Glass to recreate the way light passes through glass, generating prisms, halos, refractions, and optical blooms. It works like an "impossible lens," giving photographers and filmmakers effects they could never capture with glass alone. Pushing past the physical limitations of real-world lenses, generated with Lucid Glass. 5. Pocket Studio , by visual development artist and filmmaker Ryan McCoy Drawing on more than two decades in previsualization and visual effects for major motion pictures, Ryan McCoy built Pocket Studio to turn everyday phone footage into more polished shots. From a single take, the tool generates multiple camera angles and upgrades the visual fidelity, all while keeping the actor’s original performance intact. body:
﻿ Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services Skip to main content An official website of the United States Government Here's how you know Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock icon ) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.           the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release November 12, 2026 Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services For release at 1:30 p.m. EST Share The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services. By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services. In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks. The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org ® . Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website . For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955. Board memo (PDF) Federal Register notice (PDF) Last Update:
            November 12, 2026

While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon , excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio , the Gemini API, Gemini for business , the Gemini app , Google Search , and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity . Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs. Scaling developer and enterprise workflows Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows: Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash. Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena , arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA . Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows. Web development : On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts. Using Hydrogen for on-the-fly 3D coding, Geminisland lets anyone add to a shared voxel island from a single prompt to generate custom structures live on the map that players can walk around and explore in first person. Try the live app . Paired with our new Gemini front end design skill in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen built an e-commerce storefront in one shot complete with a WebGL2 topographic shader, pinned four-stage scrollytelling, a thermal split-slider, a 3D wireframe spec card, and a live finish configurator. Try the live app and the Gemini front end design skill . In Google Antigravity, Hydrogen turned Google Sheets into an animated pixel canvas by shrinking thousands of cells combining Python, native =LET(...) formulas, and conditional formatting to paint and animate full-motion scenes directly inside a live spreadsheet. Starting from a YouTube keynote video and a design template in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen generated a multi-slide presentation directly in Google Slides, then ran an autonomous audit-and-fix loop to catch overlapping text and clean up every slide layout. With Gemini in Google Sheets, Hydrogen can help teams rapidly turn financial data into interactive models that dynamically adjust based on various forecasting scenarios, generating outputs over 30% faster than previous models in Sheets canvas. Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens. Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations. In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth. Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details. Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list. Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe. Moving fast from idea to working prototype, Hydrogen built an interactive 3D globe and Web Audio music engine driven by real-time lightning strikes and mapped every bolt around the world into visual ripples and live ambient music. When tasked to create a WebGL2 water and glass visualizer, Hydrogen built it from pure math and SDF textures — simulating real-time light refraction, reflection, dispersion, and absorption. Using a custom skill for video assembly and adhering to a creative brief, Gemini 4 Hydrogen created an archival sizzle reel about the element ‘Hydrogen’, sourcing public-domain footage and cutting it into one continuous edit with clean narration. Hydrogen is significantly upgrading Search , delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally. Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for. More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search. Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered. Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work: Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation. Building on our commitment to reasoning transparency , Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents. Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%. For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model card . Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces: For developers: Build with the Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio , try it in AI Studio and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity . For enterprises: Deploy it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions. For everyone: Start using it in the Gemini app model drop down 1 and in Google Search for all users, and in Gemini in Google Sheets starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release November 12, 2026 Federal Reserve announces revised tentative schedule of Federal Open Market Committee meetings in 2027 For release at 12:45 p.m. EST Share The Federal Reserve on Thursday announced a revised tentative schedule of Federal Open Market Committee meetings in 2027. The Committee plans to meet on the dates listed below to discuss monetary policy and will announce its policy decision as usual on the second day of each meeting, except the October 26-27 meeting. That meeting will be dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues: January 26-27 (Tuesday-Wednesday) March 16-17 (Tuesday-Wednesday) April 27-28 (Tuesday-Wednesday) June 8-9 (Tuesday-Wednesday) July 27-28 (Tuesday-Wednesday) September 14-15 (Tuesday-Wednesday) October 26-27 (Tuesday-Wednesday) November 16-17 (Tuesday-Wednesday) January 25-26, 2028 (Tuesday-Wednesday) For media inquiries, please e-mail [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955 Last Update:
            November 12, 2026

title: From AI ambition to business impact
body: From AI ambition to business impact Nov 12, 2026 | Rodrigo Kede Lima - President, Microsoft Frontier Company Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs? That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries. Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams. More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning. The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together. What this looks like in practice Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations. 3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work while enabling scalable, auditable operations. Publicis Groupe is co-building with our engineers to bring AI into the heart of how it works and delivers for clients. Microsoft engineers work side by side with Publicis teams to design and build agentic processes grounded in Microsoft IQ, so agents work with the business context, data and knowledge behind Publicis’ work. These processes use reinforcement learning, drawing on real-world outcomes and human feedback to keep improving how the agents perform over time. The approach combines very fast engineering with hands-on knowledge transfer, helping Publicis build lasting AI capability. The work builds on Publicis’ rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 114,000 of its employees. Northern Trust needed to accelerate onboarding to its Asset Servicing Front Office Solutions platform, a process that took about two and a half weeks per client. Our engineers worked alongside Northern Trust’s experts to build an AI-powered onboarding agent within the Excel and SharePoint tools analysts already use. The result: data preparation time fell 83%, from two and a half weeks to three days, with 96.5% first pass quality score in testing . Analysts remain in control while gaining more time for higher-value client service. KT , one of South Korea’s largest telecommunications providers, wanted to help network operators identify and respond to problems faster. Our engineers worked from KT’s offices to co-build AIO-Net, a continuously learning AI agent platform informed by KT’s operating procedures and veteran network experts. It now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, while keeping people in control of decisions and actions. Saint-Gobain , the 360-year-old construction materials company, is using AI to help reduce the carbon footprint of cement. Working alongside its researchers, Microsoft engineers used Microsoft Discovery to gather 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts into a knowledge base in hours, work Saint-Gobain estimates would have taken researchers a year. In about six weeks, the team identified new hypotheses for cement additives that scientists are now testing in the lab. Across all of these customers, the pattern is the same: Begin with the value , not the technology. Redesign the process , not just the task. Build in fast cycles with the customer’s teams. Put security, governance and cost management in place from day one , so scaling doesn’t stall. This is how organizations move from isolated AI projects to sustainable transformation: by focusing on measurable outcomes, redesigning work and building the capabilities to keep improving over time. New research from IDC underscores why this approach matters. While 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across their organizations. At the same time, 71% expect AI spending to increase by at least 10% in the next year, putting even greater pressure on businesses to demonstrate measurable returns. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is reimagining how work gets done and turning that transformation into lasting business impact. We’re holding ourselves to the same standard If we’re asking customers to redesign how they work around AI, we have to do the same. Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to. The real measure of success The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build. Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours. Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company . title: We're launching a $10 million Energy Impact Program in West Virginia.
body: We're launching a $10 million Energy Impact Program in West Virginia. Nov 12, 2026 Today, we’re announcing a $10 million Energy Impact Program to support energy innovation and affordability in West Virginia. The first $1 million will go toward the West Virginia Office of Energy across six counties: Putnam, Kanawha, Cabell, Mason, Jackson, and Lincoln. Many older homes require basic repairs — like fixing roof leaks or outdated wiring — before they qualify for energy upgrades. This funding covers those essential repairs, helping qualifying families access the state Home Energy Rebate program to lower their monthly utility bills. Additionally, local governments and nonprofits will receive funding through the EECBG program for lighting, insulation, and HVAC upgrades, allowing them to redirect utility savings back into local services. This initiative is an early step in Google’s long-term investment in the communities near its planned Buffalo data center campus. To check eligibility and apply, visit energywv.org .

Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today, we are announcing the recipients of the 2026 Google PhD Fellowship Program . This year, Google.org is providing $13 million in funding to support fellowship recipients, including 148 new PhD fellows across 38 countries, deepening our commitment to the early-career scientists who are advancing the "science of AI" for the public good. The 2026 Google PhD Fellowship cohort has broad global reach, with representation across 38 countries. Foundational science with global reach Every transformative leap in technology begins the same way: with a researcher asking a bold, foundational question long before the rest of the world sees the answer. What makes this cohort extraordinary isn’t just the technical depth of their work, but the global reach and real-world ambition behind it. Around the world, these fellows are tackling problems that matter to communities everywhere: Accelerating health and life sciences: From developing representation-learning frameworks in Brazil that integrate complex genetic data to uncover disease causes, to making medical-imaging neural networks more interpretable and reliable in South Africa. Building inclusive, resilient systems: From advancing natural language processing and speech recognition for Nigerian languages, to co-designing accessible security and privacy tools for Deaf and hard-of-hearing communities in Germany. Pushing the frontiers of AI and computer hardware: From designing faster microchips that process data more efficiently in Taiwan, to creating reliable, step-by-step reasoning for language models and testing quantum theory in the lab. Direct funding and lifelong community Breakthrough science rarely happens in isolation. Beyond direct funding and access to compute which gives students the freedom to pursue high-risk, high-reward ideas, every fellow gains access to engage with Google researchers, and is welcomed into a global scientific peer network. Since 2009, the PhD Fellowship Program has supported more than 1,100 graduate students worldwide. Over the past 17 years, we have seen firsthand where that early catalyst can lead. Alumni of the program are now tenured professors, startup founders, open-source pioneers, and research leaders helping shape technology at Google itself. When we support foundational science and the emerging researchers brave enough to chart the unknown, we help build a stronger, more representative global scientific landscape for everyone. title: Scientists are using Google AI to help restore giant kelp forests.
body: Scientists are using Google AI to help restore giant kelp forests. Nov 12, 2026 Underwater forests of giant kelp protect coastlines, provide habitat, and support marine ecosystems — but they’re disappearing worldwide due to ocean warming. As COP31 kicks off this week, we’re sharing results from our partnership with Australia's national science agency, CSIRO , which is using AI and genomics to help restore giant kelp . The team recently published two high-quality reference genomes for Australian giant kelp, providing a foundation for conservation genetics work. Next researchers trained a version of Google's open-source AI tool DeepVariant to analyze giant kelp DNA. It sequenced 600 wild specimens collected from 40 sites along the Tasmanian coast, where populations have dwindled to 5% of historic numbers. This video explains how the genetic analysis and partners’ lab-based cross-breeding studies are laying the groundwork for a real-world outcome: giant kelp forests replanted with diverse, heat-tolerant specimens. This effort is part of Google Australia's Digital Futures Initiative .

title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
body: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms Nov 12, 2026 | Alysa Taylor - Chief Marketing Officer, Commercial Cloud & AI Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC , commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain. In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale. What the research found Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters. Measurement is the next test . Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms. Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks. Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy. “Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC. AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses. Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability. Where scale stalls 66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them. The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design. Inside the Frontier Firm IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause. What they do differently comes down to five behaviors: They invest ahead of plan . 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend. They deploy AI broadly , across most of the business, not just a few teams. They put agents to work . 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows. They govern so they can scale . 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters. They build skills everywhere . 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters. At Bristol Myers Squibb , the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time. Four disciplines for scaling AI value The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off. I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER . “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.” Unlock model choice Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data. Redesign workflows around agents Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters. Govern decisions and actions Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do. Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.” Measure and optimize value Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest. Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start. Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch. Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall. What this means for business The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation. First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day. Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business. Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI. The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next. Get the full picture Download the global infographic , The Real Business Value of AI, to see a summary of findings and benchmark your organization against Frontier Firms before your next AI investment review. Regional infographics are also available for Europe , Asia Pacific and the Americas . The full InfoBrief will follow. Alysa Taylor is the Chief Marketing Officer for Commercial Cloud and AI at Microsoft, leading teams that enable digital and AI transformation for organizations of all sizes across the globe. title: Barr, American Inequality and the Future of AI
body:
