Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 12, 2026 American Inequality and the Future of AI Governor Michael S. Barr At Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut Share Watch Live Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today. 1 In a speech earlier this year, I explored scenarios in which artificial intelligence (AI) could affect economic inequality, for better or for worse. 2 My focus in those remarks was on the AI side of this relationship, and today I would like to return to this topic by first providing some important context about inequality in the United States. Inequality is an aspect of every economy, and understanding the extent and evolution of inequality in the United States can help in forming a clear view of the economic outlook and how the economy is likely to react to new developments. Widening inequality may also, depending on many factors, reflect a decline in economic opportunity for many people, which can limit the economy's productive capacity. Today, I will begin by summarizing the current state of economic inequality in the United States, assisted by new results from a long-running survey of households conducted by the Federal Reserve, and then show where this fits into the history of inequality over the past century or so. I will explore some of the forces that have shaped inequality, and what these forces may indicate about how AI is likely to affect the way wealth and income are distributed. Wealth and Income Inequality Today Up-to-date and detailed information about inequality in the United States comes from the latest edition of the Federal Reserve's triennial Survey of Consumer Finances, conducted in 2025 and published just last month. 3 The survey confirms that both wealth and income are highly concentrated and that inequality is greater for wealth. The top 10 percent by income of households receive almost one-half of all income in the United States and the top 1 percent receive about one-fifth of income. 4 As for wealth, the wealthiest 10 percent of households hold nearly three-fourths of all wealth, and the top 1 percent hold about one-third. By contrast, the entire lower half of households, as measured by wealth holdings, have only 2 percent of wealth. Low wealth means it's also harder to get by every day. Another Fed survey of household finances conducted each year, the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking, finds that 31 percent of respondents in 2025 didn't have the cash to cover an emergency expense of $500 or more. 5 Wealth is even more highly concentrated among the very wealthiest. One-third of wealth is held by the upper 1 percent—that's nearly $60 trillion. There is even more concentration at the very top. The households in the upper 0.1 percent, which is only 135,000 individuals and families, own one-sixth of our nation's wealth. A household at the lower edge of the top 1 percent has 75 times as much wealth as the median household in the middle of the distribution—$16.3 million compared with $215,000 for a household in the middle. A household at the lower edge of the 0.1 percent of the wealthiest has 300 times as much wealth as the median household. Wealth concentration has increased at the very top. Using Forbes magazine's tally of the 400 wealthiest individuals, together with data from the Survey of Consumer Finances, a rough estimate is that their share of total wealth rose from 3 percent in 2022 to 4 percent in the most recent survey. Forbes counts nearly 1,000 U.S. billionaires. 6 Digging into the sources of widening inequality, the wealth of those at the top is primarily held in the form of business assets. Research using data from the Survey of Consumer Finances back to the 1940s shows that returns on business equity have been a major source of widening wealth inequality over the decades. 7 Most of the income for these wealthy households is in capital income—interest, dividends, capital gains, and business profits—rather than wages and salaries. Unlike these higher-income or wealthier households, most income for middle-class households comes from their paychecks. And it's harder to build wealth that way. Although the largest asset class for wealthy households is typically stocks and other financial assets, a substantial amount of their capital income also comes from ownership of private businesses. These private businesses come in two broad types: an actively managed business—such as a plumbing business, retail store, or manufacturing firm—and a passive investment in a business, commonly known as private equity. Owning and running a business has long been a way that households become wealthy. But private equity investments are passively run and are typically only open to the wealthiest individuals and families. These private investments have delivered returns to their owners higher than the typical mix of assets held by middle-income households. Private equity investments are 12 percent of the assets of the wealthiest 0.1 percent of households in the most recent Fed survey. For households above the median but below the 90th percentile, the most prevalent assets are housing and stocks, but the value of housing equity has grown more slowly than that of business equity. About three-fourths of households in this group have stock holdings, mostly through retirement accounts. Although ownership of publicly traded companies has become more widespread across the income spectrum as 401(k) plans have become common over the past few decades, stock ownership by value remains highly concentrated among the wealthiest households. The group of households in the 50th through the 90th percentiles of wealth hold only 17 percent of all public stocks by value, underscoring how much wealth is concentrated. 8 Finally, on net, households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution hold just over 2 percent of all wealth, an average of $52,000. About 40 percent of them have equity in homes, and nearly 40 percent own business equity, either through a retirement account or as their own business. But the values are low compared with the upper half of households. The Evolution of Inequality By many estimates, today's inequality levels are among the highest in the past 100 years. 9 But wealth and income inequality in America have changed significantly over our history, widening and, at times, also narrowing, driven by a variety of factors, including booms and busts in financial assets, structural changes in the economy, and changes in tax and regulatory policy. In the Gilded Age, roughly 1870 to 1910, incomes rose strongly for most people, but it was also the era when large fortunes were accumulated by industrialists and their families. With no income tax or estate tax for the wealthiest and limited public education for everyone, the gap between those at the top and most others widened. 10 But over the subsequent decades, especially during the New Deal, legal and institutional change strengthened worker power, and the introduction and broadening of progressive income and estate taxes helped limit the concentration of income and wealth. Inequality narrowed in the decades after World War II, an era of fast economic expansion that benefited many households. There were improvements in public education, including the GI Bill, income tax changes that made rates more progressive, and growing unionization that raised wages for workers. 11 Beginning in the late 1970s, however, wealth and income inequality began to increase again. This was a period of slower economic growth and sometimes high inflation. Top income tax rates declined, and fewer households were required to pay the estate tax. As in the 1910s and 1920s, business equity grew as a share of total assets, helping the wealthiest households become wealthier. 12 The wealth generated from the typical middle-class asset—housing—increased but at a slower pace than business assets, exacerbated by the decline in housing wealth during the Global Financial Crisis. Over the same period, real wages grew slowly. Moreover, minimum wage laws failed to keep up with inflation and the growth of the economy. 13 The lesson from this history is that the level of inequality in American society is not immutable—it changes over time. These historical patterns suggest that policy choices play a crucial role in shaping inequality levels. Economic growth, technological change, education, and globalization also play key roles. 14 The Evolution of the Labor and Capital Shares of National Income Some of these trends are most clearly seen in the decline in the share of national income going to labor over the past 25 years. Though individuals and families across the spectrum hold business equity from which they receive income, the main source of income for most households is wages and salaries—labor earnings. Since lower- and middle-income households depend heavily on wages, another useful way of exploring income and wealth inequality is to consider how the share of national income earned from labor has changed over time, compared with income earned from capital—dividends, interest, and private business earnings. After World War II, the labor share of national income was fairly steady between 60 percent and 65 percent, but it began falling in fits and starts beginning in 2001. The decline accelerated after the pandemic and has been especially steep in the past year, reaching a record low of 52.8 percent in the second quarter of 2026. 15 Some of this reflects measurement issues associated with how income has been allocated to labor and capital over time. 16 But, even after adjusting for those factors, there is a clear downward trend. Economic research suggests three causes of the decades-long trend in labor versus capital income, each highly relevant to the potential effects of AI on inequality. The first is technological innovations that have reduced demand for labor and decreased wages; the second is the concentration of market power in many industries with a small number of firms; and the third related cause is the reduction in the bargaining power of workers. Technology replacing labor has been going on for centuries, but new technology can also augment the productivity of existing jobs and create new jobs, including those that are hard to envision when the technology is initially adopted, a point I have noted in a number of speeches. 17 The internet and the businesses it created reduced employment in some occupations—such as travel agents—and eliminated others: Think video store workers. But the development of new technologies has expanded jobs in other areas. Consider that there are millions of full-time social media creators earning a living today in the United States, something unimaginable a decade ago. 18 What matters for the focus of today's discussion is how returns to labor compare with those to capital from the adoption of new technology. The available evidence from across the globe suggests that advances in digital technology have lowered the price of investment in technology relative to labor. 19 If capital is cheaper relative to labor, firms use relatively more of it. Capital can substitute for labor, too—for example, through the adoption of automation and robots. 20 Some evidence shows that firms that adopt robots may also become more productive and expand their labor force. But in this expansion, labor is outpaced by the expansion in capital, seen in rising profits and equity appreciation, which widens inequality. 21 It will be important to watch these developments closely given the immense capital investment going into the AI sector. Another factor driving the decline in the labor share of national income is market concentration, which researchers estimate has increased significantly in three-quarters of U.S. industries since 2000. Since that time, wages have grown at a slower rate than labor productivity. 22 Since larger firms are often more productive, these new technologies, in turn, can contribute to market consolidation, with so-called "superstar" firms as the result. 23 Superstar firms also have lower labor shares of income because they can establish higher product markups—the difference between their costs and what they can sell their product for—because there may be less price competition and fewer alternatives for customers. 24 At the same time, even with higher markups, their ability to deploy new technologies means these firms may be able to charge lower prices than before, which could serve to further increase their size and may result in lower costs for consumers. These forces—technological change, market concentration, and declining bargaining power for workers—may have contributed to the declining share of labor income over time. 25 All these changes have tended to favor those with the highest incomes and wealth, driving greater wealth inequality. How Will AI Affect the Labor Share of Income? The discussion of superstar firms probably brought to mind the handful of companies that are dominating AI: the hyperscalers and frontier AI labs. We have seen tremendous investment in the AI sector, with announced plans suggesting that capital deepening in this sector will escalate further. AI could be what some researchers call capital-biased innovation, in which the returns go primarily to capital rather than to labor. 26 In previous remarks, I have explored scenarios for how AI could evolve as a technology and how it could affect labor markets. Key questions include the extent to which AI will substitute for human workers—or largely complement them—and the degree to which AI will create new jobs. Market competition and the bargaining power of workers will also affect the labor share of income. The nature of AI, particularly its ability to learn how to complete complex, nonroutine tasks that require extensive knowledge difficult for humans to achieve, raises the question of whether AI's effects on the labor market will be stronger than other technologies. 27 In previous speeches I have explored whether labor displacement could be larger than in the past, and today I consider the risk that the benefits of this technological revolution could be more narrowly shared than those that came before. 28 There are questions also about the concentration of market power. Competition and distributed innovation could make AI a cheap and ubiquitous commodity, with gains widely shared. In this case, most businesses would have access to AI resources sufficient to support improved productivity and further innovation. AI could democratize access to skills and information needed for small businesses to thrive. But some researchers believe that AI has characteristics that have, in past examples of high-tech advances, reinforced concentration of market power. 29 AI depends on access to data, model improvements, and computing power, so it benefits from economies of scale and scope. AI itself is a powerful tool to train and accelerate the development of new AI models, including through self-reinforcement learning. The extent of the advantage possessed by AI leaders may prove to be unprecedented. If a small number of AI firms dominate the market and receive the lion's share of investment returns, then the wealth of the managers and owners of these firms will surge. Large businesses could afford AI investments and continue to grow, while smaller firms would see declining market share. In this scenario, the vast majority of businesses and their employees would have limited access to ever-improving AI resources, which means they would see smaller returns. Overall, the labor share of income would decline, market concentration would increase, and inequality would go up. So far, there has been relatively little displacement of workers by AI and some significant evidence that the transition to AI is enhancing the productivity of some workers, increasing demand in some sectors, and even creating new occupations. Vigorous competition among the AI firms so far has meant that access to AI remains fairly broad. Some believe that many businesses will find that most of their AI needs can be fulfilled by smaller-scale language models that will not need to be on the cutting edge of technology. And in that case, benefits would be more broadly shared. As fast as AI has grown, its implementation is still limited so far, and no one knows the degree to which its benefits will be shared. We are already seeing signs that AI may be a labor substitute in some sectors, especially for younger, less-experienced workers. Some tasks that are easily automated with clear guardrails and predictable outcomes might see rapid labor substitution, while other tasks that require human judgment, management, coordination and relationships, creativity, or outputs that are hard to measure might see more labor augmentation. 30 If labor market changes happen quickly, it will be hard for workers to adjust, and dislocations might be large, whereas a more gradual adoption might permit more orderly adjustments. That said, we should be prepared for the possibility of serious short-term disruptions in the labor market that need to be managed effectively to ensure the benefits of AI are realized over the long term. If AI proves to be capable of work that displaces humans, the extent of the disruption to the labor market will depend in part on whether society undertakes the investments needed in new job creation and worker training, connecting workers to new jobs, and other efforts to mitigate adverse effects for the long term. The concentration of market power may help drive a widening of inequality that would strain the American Dream. In my judgment, now is the time for society to begin to consider how to address these potential challenges—while AI adoption is in its relatively early stages—so we can realize the long-term benefits for society. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text 2. See Michael S. Barr (2026), "Will Artificial Intelligence Broadly Raise Living Standards or Drive Income and Wealth Inequality?" speech delivered at "Next-Gen Financial Inclusion," the third annual Financial Inclusion Conference hosted by the Federal Reserve Board, Washington, July 14. Return to text 3. Nearly 4,500 single-person households and families were interviewed. Return to text 4. The Survey of Consumer Finances measures income for the calendar year before the survey—in the most recent case, for 2024. The sources of income collected in the survey include wages, self-employment and business income, taxable and tax-exempt interest, dividends, realized capital gains, unemployment insurance, food stamps and other related support programs provided by the government, pensions and withdrawals from retirement accounts, Social Security, alimony and other support payments, and miscellaneous sources. title: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW
body: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW Plus, catch NVIDIA DLSS 5 updates for ‘War Thunder’ and ‘Where Winds Meet,’ and dive into ‘Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen,’ alongside 10 new games. November 12, 2026 by GeForce NOW Community 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to GeForce NOW , allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming. There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet . Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the GeForce NOW library this week. Kronus Calls for Reinforcements Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV , developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on Steam Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus. Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test. GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Save the storage space for everyday essentials and planning for the next offensive. Wishlist the game on Steam , and stay tuned to GFN Thursday to prepare for launch. DLSS 5 Keeps on Coming NVIDIA DLSS 5 continues to evolve, with Gaijin Entertainment’s War Thunder and Everstone Studio’s Where Winds Meet next to receive support for the technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature. Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder ’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle. In Where Winds Meet , DLSS support arrives Monday, Nov. 23, enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game. Both titles will use the latest DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model, released in October, which doubles model performance compared with the previous version. Since its initial announcement in March, model performance has improved tenfold, bringing the technology to more gamers, including GeForce NOW Ultimate members streaming with GeForce RTX 5080 cloud rigs. Get a closer look at the DLSS updates and find more details . A New Tale for the Arisen Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is streaming on GeForce NOW, expanding the deep, explorable fantasy world of Dragon’s Dogma 2 with new tales and encounters. Travel to the long-abandoned region of Norgan, join the enigmatic Eir and uncover the secrets of the undying Fallen Dragon. Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization. Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration. GeForce NOW keeps all the new downloadable content available across supported devices — without a single download claiming local storage on a gamer’s hardware of choice. In addition, members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week: Worst Class Ever (New release on Steam , Nov. 9) Ashes of the Singularity II (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Cyberpunk 2077 ( Xbox Play Anywhere, new release on Battle.net , Nov. 10) DreamWorks Shrek 2 Remastered (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Warhammer Survivors (New release on Steam and Xbox , available on Game Pass, Nov. 10) Main Sequence (New release on Steam , Nov. 12) Deadly Days: Roadtrip ( Steam ) GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend ( Steam , Ultimate members) Graveyard Keeper ( Steam ) Tape to Tape ( Steam ) Also this week, Ultimate members can take a trip back to 2006 with GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend , a playable demo celebrating the iconic GPU’s 20th anniversary with DLSS 4.5 and path tracing in the cloud. Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles. Those ready to put the next game plan into action can grab a day pass to try Performance or Ultimate, with the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership. What’s on the gaming lineup this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below. Shahram Izadi, VP and GM of XR, explains that our new Intelligent Eyewear collections from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker bring Gemini directly to your frames. These lightweight glasses help you navigate your day hands-free by providing real-time directions, language translations, and visual assistance. You can also capture photos, listen to music, and manage your schedule while keeping your phone in your pocket. Pre-orders are open now, and the glasses arrive in stores on December 10. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today, pre-orders begin for the new Intelligent Eyewear collections, made in collaboration with Gentle Monster, Warby Parker, and Samsung. With help from Gemini, these frames are ready to bring you real-time assistance throughout your day, right when you need it. 1 The new Intelligent Eyewear collections These collections, which were designed to fit a variety of styles, integrate helpful technology into frames you’ll want to wear every day, and work with Pixel and Samsung phones, as well as iPhones. 2 Gentle Monster’s high-end designs transform glasses into a means of self-expression. Their Intelligent Eyewear Collection includes six designs in bold colors — including dark red, pink, gray, and yellow — paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses. Prescription options are available for most frames. Starting at $449, the collection will be available in the United States and in South Korea. Warby Parker’s Intelligent Eyewear lineup features three refined styles — Alden, Reid, and Wren — inspired by the brand’s most beloved silhouettes, with timeless design and lightweight comfort at the forefront. You can choose from optical or sun styles starting at $395, in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colorways, with a wide range of prescription, width, and lens options. The full collection is available at warbyparker.com , and customers can sign up for a guided demo experience at more than 360 Warby Parker retail locations. Intelligent eyewear was engineered to be comfortable and helpful all day. The glasses feature lightweight frames (weighing around 41 grams) and a battery that lasts up to nine hours. 3 Each pair comes with a sleek, portable charging case that can recharge your frames up to seven times. 4 A smarter way to see the world Gemini on intelligent eyewear helps connect the dots across the Google apps and services you use every day to get you hands-free help. Just say “Hey Gemini” or tap your frames to learn the story behind a street art mural you are passing by, ask for a tailored recommendation from a “New Arrivals” bookshelf, or look at an event poster to check your Calendar availability on the spot. Gemini also helps handle your busywork in the background. Whether you’re walking between meetings or running errands with your hands full, you can ask Gemini to add what you’re looking at to your grocery list, or remind you where your next meeting is — all while keeping your eyes up and your day moving. When you’re exploring somewhere new, Google Maps delivers turn-by-turn directions in your ear. And when you ask Gemini, Google Translate will deliver real-time speech translation with automatic language detection across more than 70 languages. The glasses also feature Gemini’s new Guided Vision , which offers conversational audio descriptions to people who are blind, have low vision, or want intuitive visual assistance as they read small print or find everyday items. 5 And thanks to our collaboration with Aira , users can say “Hey Gemini, open Aira Explorer” to stream their glasses' camera feed directly to a professionally trained human visual interpreter for real-time support. Never miss a moment Custom-tuned open-ear speakers direct clear vocals and balanced audio right into your ear while keeping you fully aware of what’s around you. You can soundtrack your day with YouTube Music, Spotify, or Apple Music, and jump back into your audiobook on Audible. 6 Or use your glasses to catch up on your missed group chats, respond to messages, and take phone calls hands-free. With the integrated 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera, capturing high-quality photos and videos is as simple as pressing a button — or just asking Gemini. Your phone stays in your pocket so you can capture the moment while staying in it. HDR processing and image stabilization ensure your images and videos stay crisp, vibrant, and steady, while spatial audio capture helps you relive the moments like you were there. Privacy designed for both sides of the lens When technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too. We set out to design intelligent eyewear so that personal help doesn’t come at the expense of anyone’s privacy. You can read about our approach to privacy on intelligent eyewear in our blog , and learn more about privacy features on the Google Safety Center . Key protections include: Camera visuals from Gemini on glasses are not saved in your Gemini History and aren’t used to train AI models or target ads. Your glasses are also designed to automatically redact bystanders’ faces from these visuals before Gemini processes them. title: Designing for privacy on intelligent eyewear
body: Designing for privacy on intelligent eyewear Nov 12, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Our new intelligent eyewear can give you fast answers about what you see, all while staying hands free. Learn more about how we’re building eyewear designed to protect the privacy of you and the people around you. Shahram Izadi VP & GM, XR Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary Shahram Izadi, VP and GM of XR, explains how we are building privacy protections into intelligent eyewear to safeguard both wearers and bystanders. These features include physical indicator lights, automatic face redaction, and strict data encryption to ensure your information remains secure. You can visit the Google Safety Center to learn more about our approach to privacy and how we handle data across our wearable devices. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Shahram Izadi, VP and GM of XR, explains how we prioritize privacy for both wearers and bystanders. We do not save camera visuals in Gemini History, nor do we use them for model training. You control your data through app permissions, chat history settings, and a physical power off switch. An outward LED indicator light alerts people nearby when you capture photos or record video footage. Our glasses automatically redact faces and use directional microphones to focus solely on your own voice. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Shahram Izadi, VP and GM of XR, explains that our intelligent eyewear uses Gemini to help you translate signs, read menus, and navigate your day. We built these glasses with privacy for everyone in mind, including physical indicator lights for bystanders and automatic face redaction. Your visual data is encrypted, never used for ads, and not saved in your history. You also keep full control over your settings and can turn the device off anytime. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Intelligent eyewear with Gemini 1 can help you understand another language, make sense of a confusing parking sign, or know when to take the next step in your recipe, all thanks to its ability to see what you see. And with experiences like Guided Vision in Gemini Live , these glasses can provide audio descriptions to people who are blind or have low vision as they read small print or find everyday items. 2 But when technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too. Throughout our years of research on glasses, we listened closely to wearers, bystanders, and privacy experts. We found that wearers were constantly calculating using glasses like these out-and-about during their day, while bystanders noted concerns about being filmed without their knowledge. This led us to the conviction that privacy protections on glasses must cover both the person behind the lenses and those in front of them. Privacy designed for both sides of the lens With this in mind, we set out to design the glasses so that personal help doesn’t come at the expense of anyone’s privacy. Here are some of the key features we’ve built into both the hardware and software to protect wearers and those nearby. Protecting your visual data Camera visuals aren’t saved in your Gemini History . When you ask Gemini on glasses about the world around you, like getting help translating a menu in another language, the camera visuals are not saved in your Gemini History. 3 Camera visuals aren’t used for AI training or ad targeting. The visuals Gemini captures are used to give you answers or get you the help you need. They are not used to train AI models or target ads. Your data is encrypted. Data stored on glasses is encrypted, and if data leaves your glasses — like for processing on your phone or in the cloud — it’s also encrypted in transit to keep it private and secure. Coming soon, we’re also bringing Private AI Compute technology to glasses to process data in a secure, fortified space in addition to our other safeguards. You choose what you share You choose what apps can access your camera. Giving apps access to your glasses camera can be really helpful, like if you want to sync your audiobook app with the last page you read in your paperback copy. But before any app can access your camera for the first time, it asks for your permission. After that, you stay in control, and you can grant or revoke access anytime for each individual app. You control your Gemini history. Your chats are saved in Gemini History so you can pick up a conversation where you left off and get more personalized help. You control your personalization and history settings, so you can review past interactions, delete individual chats, or even delete all of them. You can also control in settings whether the text of your chats is used to improve generative AI models. Learn more about how your Gemini data is handled in the Gemini Apps Privacy Hub . Every pair has an off switch. And of course, you have a physical power switch on the frames to turn your glasses completely off whenever you want to wear them as regular glasses only. Privacy protections for those around you Every pair of glasses has an outer indicator light. We’ve heard from bystanders that the most helpful feature for them is a clear indication that the glasses are recording photos and videos. When you take a photo or video for your gallery, an outward-facing LED indicator lights up to let people around you know. The indicator light is designed not to be messed with . If the indicator light is covered or tampered with, sensors are designed to detect that and prevent photos or videos from being taken. The glasses are designed to redact faces before sending images to Gemini. When you ask Gemini a question, there may be others nearby. Not only are these Gemini visuals not used for AI model training, your glasses are also designed to automatically redact bystanders’ faces before Gemini processes the visuals. Gemini is designed to focus on your voice. We’ve also designed Gemini to focus on your voice by default, and not other voices around you, using directional microphones on the glasses. These are a few examples of the privacy features built into the intelligent eyewear experience. Learn more about our approach in the Google Safety Center . Protections and restrictions across Google In addition to these features, there are also protections across Google apps and services to deter misuse of the glasses. Responsible use requirements: Before using intelligent eyewear, users must agree not to record others without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the outer indicator light. Not following these requirements is a violation of the Google Terms of Service, and a user’s ability to use the glasses may be disabled. Google Shopping and Google Ads: Policies do not allow the promotion of products and services that disable or hide recording indicator lights on smart glasses. Google Play : Policies prohibit apps from using the camera for social live-streaming or real-time facial identification, and from changing the behavior of the outer indicator light. YouTube: Policies prohibit content that depicts things like harassment and unwanted sexualization. Any video uploaded to YouTube — whether it’s recorded on a phone, a camera, or glasses — has to follow these policies, and videos that don’t are removed. Account restrictions: Intelligent eyewear devices are designed to be set up only with compatible 18+ Google Accounts. This is just the beginning. Privacy is foundational to how we design, build, and evolve wearable technology. As glasses become more capable, our focus is on creating helpful experiences that make both wearers and bystanders feel protected. We look forward to advancing this work in collaboration with privacy experts and others across the ecosystem to further protections for everyone on both sides of the lens. title: We’re introducing a new transparency tool for invalid traffic in Google Ads.
body: Google Ads We’re introducing a new transparency tool for invalid traffic in Google Ads. Keerat Sharma VP & General Manager, Ads Privacy and Safety Nov 12, 2026 We’ve long built defenses directly into our ad systems to block invalid traffic, helping businesses get the most out of their budgets and spend with confidence. Today, we’re rolling out the Invalid Traffic Overview Card in Google Ads to give advertisers front-end transparency into how we protect their campaigns. We don’t charge for invalid traffic, and our multi-layered defenses have always worked in the background to catch it before an advertiser is billed. We issue a credit when it’s detected later, where appropriate and possible. Now, for the first time, businesses can see both the amount saved and the credits we automatically provide for invalid activity in Google Ads. As bad actors become more sophisticated, we’re continually strengthening our approach to keep policy violators off our platforms. So far in 2026, we’ve reduced advertiser exposure to invalid leads by an average of 30% through continuous system upgrades.
retained_feed_body: Google Ads introduces the Invalid Traffic Overview Card for campaign transparency. See your savings and credits from November 2026. Get the details.

title: Champaign County man sentenced to 15 years in prison for distributing child pornography
body: Press Release Champaign County man sentenced to 15 years in prison for distributing child pornography Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Ohio DAYTON, Ohio – Christopher Creamer, 40, of Urbana, was sentenced in U.S. District Court today to 180 months in prison, followed by a 15-year term of supervised release, for distributing child pornography. According to court documents, from June to August 2025, Creamer communicated online with an individual he believed to be a Telegram user but was actually an FBI agent. Creamer distributed two images and 16 videos of child pornography to the agent. He also discussed his interest in the sexual abuse of children. In a subsequent search of Creamer’s electronic devices, agents discovered more than 3,000 images and 130 videos depicting child pornography, including images of the sexual abuse of infants and toddlers and sadomasochistic conduct. Creamer further admitted that he previously sexually abused a 14-year-old victim. Creamer was arrested and charged by federal criminal complaint in March and pleaded guilty in July. Dominick S. Gerace II, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio, and Jason Cromartie, Special Agent in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cincinnati Division,  announced the sentence imposed today by Senior U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Rose. Assistant United States Attorney Christina E. Mahy is representing the United States in this case. This case is part of Project Safe Childhood , a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. # # # Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Ohio, Southern

Tallahassee Felon Pleads Guilty to Federal Firearm Offense
body: Press Release Tallahassee Felon Pleads Guilty to Federal Firearm Offense Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Tallahassee, Florida – Etavious J. Milton, 27, of Tallahassee, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “The Tallahassee Police Department deserves particular recognition for taking this dangerous criminal off our streets, and thanks to the successful prosecution by my office we will ensure he remains behind federal bars as long as possible. Our citizens deserve to live in safe, crime-free neighborhoods, and my office will deliver on that promise by incapacitating the dangerous criminals who have preyed upon our communities for far too long.” Court documents reflect that at approximately 3:00 a.m. on January 17, 2026, the defendant attempted to flee from law enforcement after committing a traffic violation. The defendant crashed the vehicle he was driving, after narrowly avoiding hitting another vehicle. While waiting for an ambulance, officers stabilized the defendant and observed a black Beretta 9mm caliber pistol near his waist. The officers secured the firearm, and the defendant was then taken to the hospital after emergency medical personnel arrived on scene.  As a previously convicted felon, the defendant was prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition. Milton faces up to 15 years imprisonment. The case involved a joint investigation by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and the Tallahassee Police Department. Assistant United States Attorney Eric Welch is prosecuting the case. Sentencing is scheduled for January 22, 2027 at 11:00 a.m. at the United States Courthouse in Tallahassee before United States District Judge Mark Walker. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities . The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access available public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl . Contact United States Attorney’s Office Northern District of Florida USAFLN.Press.Office@usdoj.gov X: @USAO_NDFL Updated November 12, 2026 Topics Project Safe Neighborhoods Firearms Offenses Components Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) USAO - Florida, Northern

title: Firearms Smugglers Sentenced in Del Rio to Combined 39.5 Years in Federal Prison
body: Press Release Firearms Smugglers Sentenced in Del Rio to Combined 39.5 Years in Federal Prison Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Texas DEL RIO, Texas – Two Americans and an illegal alien from Mexico were sentenced in a federal court in Del Rio on Tuesday to a combined 474 months in prison for their roles in a firearms trafficking conspiracy, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. According to court documents, Edgar Josue Montelongo-Loera, 39, of Dallas, and Reymundo Hernandez-Nino, 41, an illegal alien from Mexico were determined to be responsible for the trafficking of firearms to Mexico. In August 2024, agents from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) received information that Montelongo-Loera’s sister and Hernande-Nino’s wife, Kenia Lizbeth Montelongo, 31, had purchased multiple firearms including seven .380 caliber pistols and a .22 caliber pistol between May 17, 2024, and July 5, 2024. In the days following each of the purchases, Montelongo crossed into Mexico through Laredo. Montelongo-Loera, who had displayed multiple firearms in his social media profile pictures, was also recorded crossing in the same vehicle. USA v. Hernandez-Nino et. al. Case 2:25cr1979 In August 2024, ATF agents reviewed WhatsApp conversations that included Montelongo-Loera, in which he said his “buddy” could get requested firearms and that he had someone who could transport them. ATF agents reviewed additional WhatsApp conversations in November 2024, in which Montelongo-Loera again discussed his firearm trafficking operation. Montelongo-Loera was arrested on July 14, 2025, after a co-conspirator was found attempting to smuggle eight handguns and 19 magazines into Mexico. Two days later, ATF agents, along with the San Antonio Police Department, and ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations, executed a search warrant on the San Antonio residence of Hernandez-Nino. A total of 24 firearms were immediately recovered, to include handguns, AR-15 style assault rifles, and a shotgun. ATF also recovered more than 4,000 rounds of ammunition from the residence and multiple sets of body armor. Based on other evidence obtained during the investigation, ATF determined that the weapons, ammunition and accessories were bound for a Mexican drug cartel. Hernandez-Nino and Kenia Lizbeth Montelongo were arrested during the search. Montelongo-Loera pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to traffic firearms on Feb. 23. On Feb. 26, Hernandez-Nino pleaded guilty to smuggling goods from the United States and alien in possession of a firearm, while Kenia Lizbeth Montelongo pleaded guilty to smuggling goods from the United States and sale or transfer to a prohibited person. On Tuesday, Chief U.S. District Judge Alia Moses sentenced Montelongo-Loera to 180 months in federal prison. Hernandez-Nino and Kenia Montelongo were sentenced to 150 and 144 months, respectively. “These three sentencings bring to a close a massive case involving ten conspirators who smuggled more than 200 weapons into Mexico,” said U.S. Attorney Simmons. “This activity is orchestrated by cartels, and the weapons being trafficked across the border are in direct support of organized criminal activity. Specifically, these weapons are used by cartels to terrorize Mexican citizens and war with law enforcement in an effort to maintain control of drug trafficking and human smuggling routes. These activities ultimately harm American citizens trapped in the prison of addiction and facilitate the movement of illegal aliens with violent criminal history into our country, our cities, and our neighborhoods. My office has a long history of aggressively prosecuting those who smuggle firearms, and we will continue to aggressively prosecute those who violate American laws at the behest of the Mexican cartels.” “This investigation demonstrates ATF’s unwavering commitment to identifying, disrupting, and dismantling firearms trafficking networks that fuel violence across our borders,” said Special Agent in Charge Michael Weddel for ATF Houston. “These defendants played significant roles in a coordinated operation to illegally acquire and traffic firearms intended for a Mexican drug cartel. Through the dedicated work of our special agents and our law enforcement partners, we were able to uncover this operation, seize dozens of firearms, and hold those responsible accountable. ATF will continue to aggressively pursue those who exploit our firearms laws and facilitate the flow of illegal weapons into the hands of criminal organizations.” Assistant U.S. Attorney Brett Miner prosecuted the case. This case was investigated and prosecuted by the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) as part of Operation Take Back America . HSTFs, which were established by President Trump in Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion, are joint operations led by the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security. body: Press Release California Man Sentenced to 15 Years in Federal Prison  for Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Dakota RAPID CITY - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Camela T. Theeler has sentenced a Rapid City, South Dakota, man convicted of Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance.  The sentencing took place on November 10, 2026. Martin Ramirez, 45, was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison, followed by five years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. Ramirez was indicted for Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance by a federal grand jury in July 2025.  He pleaded guilty on September 1, 2026. In 2022, Ramirez connected with individuals in western South Dakota to distribute methamphetamine.  He was ultimately responsible for sending or receiving several pounds of methamphetamine and further distributing it to individuals involved in the conspiracy. This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.  Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETFs) and Project Safe Neighborhood (PSN).  Through PSN, the District of South Dakota seeks to bring together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce gun violence and make our neighborhoods safer for everyone. This case was investigated by the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Unified Narcotics Enforcement Team (UNET), and the Drug Enforcement Administration. UNET is comprised of law enforcement from the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, the Rapid City Police Department, South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, the South Dakota Highway Patrol and the South Dakota National Guard.  Assistant U.S. Attorneys Edward C. Tarbay and Megan Poppen prosecuted the case. Ramirez was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service. title: Navarre Woman Sentenced to Five Years in Federal Prison for Drug Trafficking
body: Press Release Navarre Woman Sentenced to Five Years in Federal Prison for Drug Trafficking Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Pensacola, Florida – Loredana Alessandra Bassolino, 38, of Navarre, Florida was sentenced to five years in federal prison after previously pleading guilty to possession with intent to distribute more than 40 grams of fentanyl and more than 5 grams of methamphetamine. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Thanks to the excellent investigative work of the DEA, with support from the Gulf Coast HIDTA and our U.S. Marshals, and this successful prosecution by my office, this drug trafficker will be kept off our streets. President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche remain fully committed to delivering the safe, drug-free communities that our citizens deserve, and my office will fulfill that promise with aggressive prosecutions like this one to hold the peddlers of deadly drugs accountable.” Court documents reflect that on January 14, 2026, federal agents executed an arrest warrant for Andre Perry at a hotel in Pensacola, Florida. When law enforcement made entry into Perry’s hotel room to effectuate the arrest, they observed drug paraphernalia littered throughout the room, along with a “speed loader” tool used to quickly load ammunition into firearm magazines. Bassolino, another occupant of the hotel room, admitted that narcotics were present and gave consent to search the room. During their search, law enforcement discovered fentanyl, methamphetamine, and a loaded firearm. Both Bassolino and Perry are convicted felons who are legally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition, with Perry most recently being convicted of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and fentanyl and possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine and fentanyl in July 2025. “Fentanyl remains the biggest drug threat facing our country,” said Special Agent in Charge Daniel Escobar, DEA Tampa Field Division. “Our agents and law enforcement partners remain vigilant in the fight to rid our communities of traffickers who distribute this poison to our citizens.” Perry is scheduled for sentencing on February 11, 2027, at 2:00 pm before United States District Judge T. Kent Wetherell, II in Pensacola, Florida. The conviction and sentence were the result of an investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration with assistance from the United States Marshals Service and the Gulf Coast High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA) Task Force. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Thomas S.P. Geeker. title: Pekin Man Sentenced to 46 Months in Prison for Possession of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Pekin Man Sentenced to 46 Months in Prison for Possession of Child Pornography Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of Illinois PEORIA, Ill. – A Pekin, Illinois, man, Jeffrey L. Gualandi, Jr., 33, was sentenced on October 27, 2026, to 46 months in prison, to be followed by five years of supervised release, for possession of child pornography. He must also register as a sex offender and pay restitution to victims identified in the images under the provisions of the Amy, Vicky, and Andy Child Pornography Victim Assistance Act of 2018. At the sentencing hearing, it was established that in July 2024 in Tazewell County, Illinois, Gualandi possessed multiple electronic devices that contained images of child pornography. Law enforcement officers executed a search warrant that month at Gualandi’s Pekin residence and found six electronic devices that contained 653 images classified as child sexual abuse material. Gualandi was indicted in May 2025 and pleaded guilty in February 2026. The statutory penalties for possession of child pornography are not more than 20 years in prison, not more than a $250,000 fine, and at least a five-year to life term of supervised release. In sentencing the defendant, U.S. District Judge Jonathan E. Hawley noted the seriousness of the offense because it involved real victims. “These types of cases will be vigorously prosecuted by this Office because of the ongoing trauma they cause these vulnerable children. They are first victimized by the producer of the images and subsequently victimized each time the image is viewed,” said Assistant United States Attorney Melissa P. Ortiz. “Those who collect and possess child sexual abuse material help perpetuate the abuse of children and will be held accountable for their actions,” said FBI Springfield Field Office Special Agent in Charge Ryan Presley. “This sentence is the result of the strong partnership between the FBI Springfield Field Office, the Pekin Police Department, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office in our shared mission to investigate these crimes and pursue justice for victims.” The Pekin Police Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Springfield Field Office, investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa P. Ortiz and Douglas F. McMeyer represented the government in the prosecution. The case against Gualandi was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative by the Department of Justice to combat the epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov. title: LAFAYETTE MAN SENTENCED TO 37 MONTHS IN FEDERAL PRISON FOR CYBERSTALKING
body: Press Release LAFAYETTE MAN SENTENCED TO 37 MONTHS IN FEDERAL PRISON FOR CYBERSTALKING Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Louisiana Anthony Joseph Depa, age 49, of Lafayette, Louisiana, was sentenced to 37 months in federal prison following his conviction for cyberstalking. U.S. District Judge John W. deGravelles further sentenced Depa to serve three years of supervised release following his term of imprisonment. According to admissions made as part of his guilty plea, beginning in January 2025 and continuing through the end of March 2025, Depa repeatedly threatened, harassed, and intimidated several victims in the Middle District of Louisiana and elsewhere, by sending them a series of electronic messages (including email messages, text messages, and messages through a social media platform), in which he threatened to kill and harm the individuals and members of their families. For instance, in an email Depa sent to several of his victims on January 26, 2025, he told the victims, in part, “I will kill all 3 of you when I see you in person next. . . . Not a threat. A f****** promise.”  In another message, he told one of his victims that he would “jump into” the victim’s “window” and “end [the victim’s] life.” Depa continued sending threatening messages even after one of the victims obtained two restraining orders against him in state court, telling the victims that he would “beat [them] to death . . . with [his] bare hands” and “kill them,” and that he would “sneak into [one victim’s] window” and “rape” his wife. U.S. Attorney Kurt L. Wall praised the work of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Ascension Parish Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Alan A. Stevens, who serves as Senior Litigation Counsel for the Criminal Division, leads the prosecution. Updated November 12, 2026 Component USAO - Louisiana, Middle

title: Sumter Man Sentenced to Federal Prison After Flying Drone Over South Carolina Prison
body: Press Release Sumter Man Sentenced to Federal Prison After Flying Drone Over South Carolina Prison Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Carolina COLUMBIA, S.C. — Quinzell Robinson, 47, of Sumter, has been sentenced to one year and one day in federal prison for flying a drone onto a South Carolina prison yard. On March 14, 2025, at 5 a.m., law enforcement responded to reports of a drone flying near Lieber Correctional Facility in Ridgeville. Investigators located Robinson leaving the woods near the facility with a drone and a bag. After reviewing surveillance footage, investigators learned that shortly after 5 a.m., a package was dropped onto prison grounds and retrieved by inmates. Investigators sought and obtained authorization to search the electronic devices seized from Robinson on March 14, 2025, including the drone. The drone’s flight data showed that it traveled to the location where LCI surveillance captured the inmates recovering a package. A forensic analysis of a seized cell phone revealed aerial photographs of LCI, numerous web searches related to purchasing drones, and GPS data from where the drone was launched on March 14, 2025. Investigators also found several video recordings filmed on the device, including a video that appeared to show a flight over a correctional facility, and text messages with an LCI inmate about using drones to deliver contraband to the prison and anti-drone measures used by prisons. "Correctional facilities cannot safely operate when individuals on the outside coordinate with inmates to deliver contraband over prison fences using drones,” said U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling for the District of South Carolina. “This case sends a clear message that those who attempt to use technology to undermine prison security will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable for their actions.” "We are under nightly attacks by drones dropping deadly drugs and other contraband onto our prison yards," SCDC Director Joel Anderson said. "I appreciate the courts and our law enforcement partners for holding him accountable.” United States District Judge Richard M. Gergel sentenced Robinson to one year and one day in federal prison for knowingly and willfully operating an unregistered aircraft under Federal Aviation Administration laws. United States District Judge Richard M. Gergel sentenced Robinson to one year and one day in federal prison for knowingly and willfully operating an unregistered aircraft under Federal Aviation Administration laws. This case was investigated by United States Department of Transportation Office of Inspector General, the South Carolina Department of Corrections Office of Inspector General, and the Dorchester County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Winston Holliday prosecuted the case. ### Updated November 12, 2026 Component USAO - South Carolina

Myers, with engaging in, and attempting to engage in, illicit sexual conduct with minors in Haiti. According to court documents, Osbeck routinely traveled from the U.S. to Haiti over the past three decades and sexually abused minors in that country. body: Press Release Jacksonville Pharmacy Owner and Accountant Indicted in $51 Million  Health Care Fraud Scheme Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Florida Jacksonville, Florida – Charlie Bernard Griffin III (61, Jacksonville) has been charged in a 31-count federal indictment with health care fraud and money laundering. Ethelbert Chinenye Nwanegbo (47, St. Johns) has been charged in the same indictment with money laundering. Each faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison on each count. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement. The indictment notifies Griffin that the United States is seeking an order of forfeiture in the amount of $14,245,474, representing Griffin’s proceeds from the health care fraud, and an order of forfeiture in the amount of $17,807,628.14, representing the property involved in the money laundering offenses with which he is charged. The indictment also notifies Griffin that the United States is seeking forfeiture of a total of $8,182,800.17 that was seized from Griffin’s bank accounts, along with three real properties and four vehicles Griffin purchased with fraud proceeds. The indictment notifies Nwanegbo that the United States is seeking an order of forfeiture in the amount of $6,068,540.50, representing the property involved in the money laundering offenses with which he is charged. According to the indictment, Griffin owned First Coast Community Development (FCCD), which operated a pharmacy in Jacksonville. Griffin entered into an agreement with a marketing company owned by Jonathan Gholston pursuant to which the company referred people to FCCD for the provision of HIV post-exposure prophylactic medications. Representatives of the marketing company set up tents and tables in Jacksonville, generally in low-income areas, and offered to provide free, government-sponsored cellphones to anyone who stopped and agreed to provide identifying information. As a result of the marketing company’s agreement with FCCD, while obtaining the personal information necessary for the person to receive the free cellphone, the marketing representatives also obtained health insurance information, including whether the person was covered by Medicare, Medicaid, or a private insurer. The agreement provided that FCCD would pay the marketing company $200 for every person who was referred for HIV medications, but that FCCD would pay this amount only if a claim submitted on behalf of the person was paid by Medicare, Medicaid, or a private insurance company. The marketing company paid its representatives a set amount, usually $50, for every person who was referred to FCCD for HIV medications, but it paid this amount only if a claim submitted on behalf of the person was paid. A marketer’s being paid per referral based upon whether a claim is paid is an illegal kickback. The information gathered by the marketing representatives was sent to FCCD and its pharmacist, Albert Chester. FCCD used the information to generate prescriptions for HIV medications that were authorized by Rashan Jones, a nurse practitioner who had never seen, spoken with, or performed any manner of evaluation, examination, or test on the persons for whom the prescriptions were issued. To ensure that FCCD’s claims for the prescriptions were paid, FCCD falsely and fraudulently used a diagnosis code reflecting that the persons to whom the prescriptions were issued had, or had been exposed to, HIV or a sexually transmitted disease, a false diagnosis that was documented in the medical records of the persons who were issued the prescriptions. FCCD filled the prescriptions, submitted claims to Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurers for the medications, and, if the claims were paid, was reimbursed for the medications. The actions of Griffin and his co-conspirators caused the submission of tens of thousands of fraudulent claims, resulting in reimbursements from Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers totaling approximately $51 million. Griffin received a total of approximately $14 million in proceeds as a result of his involvement in the offense. Gholston, Chester, and Jones were previously charged separately and each of them agreed to plead guilty. Nwanegbo was an accountant in Jacksonville. After Griffin and a co-conspirator received proceeds of the health care fraud scheme, they transferred and deposited proceeds into accounts controlled by Nwanegbo. For some of the proceeds, Nwanegbo transferred the funds from those accounts to other accounts he controlled. Nwanegbo then returned the proceeds to Griffin and the co-conspirator by transferring and depositing the proceeds into other accounts controlled by Griffin and the co-conspirator and by making cash payments to them, after retaining a money laundering fee of approximately 10%. This case is being investigated by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services – Office of Inspector General and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Arnold B. Corsmeier. The forfeiture is being handled by Assistant United States Attorney Clint Locke. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. Updated November 12, 2026 Topics Financial Fraud Healthcare Fraud Component USAO - Florida, Middle
retained_feed_body: Jacksonville, Florida – Charlie Bernard Griffin III (61, Jacksonville) has been charged in a 31-count federal indictment with health care fraud and money laundering. Ethelbert Chinenye Nwanegbo (47, St. Johns) has been charged in the same indictment with money laundering. Each faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison on each count. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

title: Arizona Man Sentenced to 14 Years in Federal Prison  for Conspiracy to Distribute Controlled Substances into South Dakota
body: Press Release Arizona Man Sentenced to 14 Years in Federal Prison  for Conspiracy to Distribute Controlled Substances into South Dakota Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Dakota RAPID CITY - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Camela T. Theeler has sentenced a Tucson, Arizona, man convicted of Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance.  The sentencing took place on November 9, 2026. Francisco Siquieros-Valenzuela, also known as “Pancho,” 32, was sentenced to 14 years in federal prison, followed by five years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. Siquieros-Valenzuela was indicted for Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance by a federal grand jury in September 2025.  He pleaded guilty on May 20, 2026. The defendant was part of a multi-state drug conspiracy involving persons from Mexico, Arizona, and South Dakota responsible for importing primarily fentanyl and methamphetamine and then shipping it from Arizona to South Dakota.  Ultimately, over 1 kilogram of fentanyl pills (more than 10,000 pills) were shipped into the State. “We found this guy in Tucson,” said U.S. Attorney Parsons.  “He was sourcing fentanyl and methamphetamine out of Mexico, packaging it up, and sending it our way to poison our communities.  Let me be clear: anyone who ships illegal drugs to South Dakota, whether they ever actually set foot here or not, will be identified, tracked down, apprehended, prosecuted, and shipped off themselves to federal prison.” This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETFs) and Project Safe Neighborhood (PSN). Through PSN, the District of South Dakota seeks to bring together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce gun violence and make our neighborhoods safer for everyone. This case was investigated by Drug Enforcement Administration, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Rapid City Police Department, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.  Criminal Chief Gregg Peterman prosecuted the case. Siquieros-Valenzuela was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service. Contact usasd.press@usdoj.gov Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Operation Take Back America Component USAO - South Dakota

title: Mission Man Sentenced to 25 Years in Federal Prison  for Second Degree Murder and Assault with a Dangerous Weapon
body: Press Release Mission Man Sentenced to 25 Years in Federal Prison  for Second Degree Murder and Assault with a Dangerous Weapon Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Dakota PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced a Rapid City, South Dakota, man convicted of Second Degree Murder and Assault with a Dangerous Weapon.  The sentencing took place on November 9, 2026. Lucas Guerue, age 28, was sentenced to 25 years in federal prison, followed by five years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund for Second Degree Murder.  Guerue was sentenced to eight years in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund for Assault with a Dangerous Weapon. The sentences will be served concurrently. Guerue was indicted by a federal grand jury in May 2025 and pleaded guilty on August 13, 2026. The convictions stem from an incident that occurred within the Rosebud Sioux Indian Reservation. On March 20, 2025, sometime after 2:00 a.m., Guerue was drinking whiskey from a bottle while driving around in a Buick with a friend, when he saw the victims in a Chevrolet Traverse.  He quickly turned around and began to follow them.  Earlier that day, Guerue threatened to shoot the driver of the Traverse.  Guerue pursued the vehicle at high speeds on U.S. Highway 18 between Rosebud and Mission.  He then accelerated and intentionally rammed the back end of the Traverse at 118 miles per hour with the specific purpose of hurting its occupants.  His purpose was achieved.  The collision caused the Traverse to careen into the ditch and begin to roll.  The driver was thrown from the vehicle and killed.  The passenger was thrown from the vehicle and suffered severe injuries.  Guerue fled the scene but was later apprehended. This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian country be prosecuted in federal court as opposed to State court. This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Kimberly Zachrison prosecuted the case. Guerue was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service. Contact usasd.press@usdoj.gov Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Indian Country Law and Justice Component USAO - South Dakota

title: One of the last members of Great Falls meth trafficking ring pleads guilty
body: Press Release One of the last members of Great Falls meth trafficking ring pleads guilty Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Montana GREAT FALLS – One of the last defendants in a far-reaching drug ring investigation based out of Great Falls admitted to charges today, U.S. Attorney Scott Twito said. Leland Neal Lapier, Jr., 42, pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine. Lapier faces 15 years to life in prison, at least 10 years of supervised release, a $20 million fine, and a $100 special assessment. Chief U.S. District Judge Brian M. Morris presided and will determine a sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Sentencing was set for March 17, 2027.  Lapier was released subject to conditions pending further proceedings. The government alleged in court documents that Lapier was linked to a drug trafficking organization run out of Great Falls by, among others, Dan Wakeford and Mike Wakeford . In 2024, investigators seized over 100 pounds of meth and an illegal firearm in an Arizona storage unit connected to this conspiracy. Law enforcement learned in its investigation that Lapier supplied methamphetamine to Dan Wakeford starting around 2020. For roughly the next year, Lapier provided Wakeford with an estimated 30 to 80 pounds of meth at $8,000 a pound. Eventually, the price of the meth changed and Dan Wakeford stopped using Lapier and started using his brother Mike Wakeford to source their meth. Dan Wakeford was later arrested and so Mike Wakeford connected with Lapier. The two worked together buying and trafficking meth until Mike Wakeford was arrested in May 2025. Lapier, who continued to traffic meth, was arrested in Great Falls in February 2026.  Law enforcement learned that multiple other individuals both provided and received methamphetamine from Lapier during this period. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeff Starnes and Zeno Baucus are prosecuting the case. The investigation was conducted by the Russell Country Drug Task Force, including the FBI and DEA. This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Montana comprises agents and officers from the DEA, FBI, ATF, HSI, the Montana Division of Criminal Investigation, the Great Falls Police Department, and the Cascade County Sheriff’s Office with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Montana. Contact Keri Leggett Acting Public Affairs Officer keri.leggett@usdoj.gov Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Homeland Security Task Force Components Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Montana Press Release Number: 266-300
