title: Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency
body: Press Release Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of California North Korean Super Intelligence-Enabled Social Engineering Campaign Known as “FaceStealer” Targeted Cryptocurrency Holders and Individuals Working the Open-Source Supply Chain LOS ANGELES – Today, the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange. “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.” “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.” “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.” “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.” “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.” “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.” Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain. North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust. During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts. The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims. The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer , to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme. The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant United States Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki of the National Security Division and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. The Justice Department, the FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars’ Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen from Binance Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount. Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the United States Secret Service (USSS) and IRS Criminal Investigation, issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets. The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and IRS Criminal Investigation. Contact Ciaran McEvoy Public Information Officer ciaran.mcevoy@usdoj.gov (213) 894-4465 Updated November 12, 2026 Topics Cybercrime Fraud Securities, Commodities, & Investment Fraud Countering Nation-State Threats National Security Component USAO - California, Central Press Release Number: 26-217

title: Felon Pleads Guilty to Unlawfully Selling Firearms and Ammunition Without a Federal Firearms License
body: Press Release Felon Pleads Guilty to Unlawfully Selling Firearms and Ammunition Without a Federal Firearms License Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nevada LAS VEGAS – A Las Vegas man who has prior felony convictions pleaded guilty today to unlawfully selling over a dozen firearms without a Federal Firearms License. According to court documents, from about April 30, 2025, to about June 17, 2025, Gregory Urbanek possessed and sold 14 firearms, including shotguns, rifles, and pistols, and a 100-round magazine without a Federal Firearms License. He has previous felony convictions of attempted grand larceny, possession of a firearm by an ex-felon, and trafficking in a controlled substance, all in Clark County, Nevada. He is prohibited by law from possessing firearms and ammunition. “Let me be crystal clear: when a convicted felon turns our neighborhoods into an underground gun market, they are putting a target on the back of every law-abiding citizen in this community,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “Bypassing federal background checks to flood our streets with untraceable weapons and ammunition is not a victimless paperwork crime—it is a direct pipeline for violent crime. My office and our ATF partners will relentlessly hunt down, dismantle, and lock up anyone who profits off illegal firearms trafficking.” “ATF takes any threat to the safety of the public seriously,” said Special Agent in Charge John Wester, San Francisco Field Division, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives (ATF). “Protecting the public is our mission. We are committed to ensuring that Las Vegas is a safe place. If you are a prohibited person and you obtain firearms or ammunition, we will hold you accountable. If you are firearms trafficking, we will hold you accountable. The suspect in this case is a prohibited person. He possessed and sold multiple firearms and ammunition without a Federal Firearms License. This kind of illegal and dangerous conduct will not be tolerated.  ATF is committed to working alongside our partners at the U.S. Attorney’s Office to ensure crimes of this nature are brought to justice.” Urbanek pleaded guilty to one count of engaging in the business of dealing in firearms without a license and three counts of felon in possession of a firearm. The total statutory maximum penalty is 50 years in prison. Sentencing is scheduled on February 10, 2027, before United States District Judge Gloria M. Navarro. The ATF investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Tina Snellings is prosecuting the case. The public may submit anonymous tips about gun crimes to ATF by calling 1-888-ATF-TIPS (1-888-283-8477) or by submitting a tip online at www.atf.gov/contact/atf-tips . ### Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Nevada

title: International Law Enforcement Operation Targeting Opioid and Fentanyl Traffickers on the Dark Web Results in over 350 Arrests Worldwide and the Seizure of Drugs, Weapons, and over $234 Million
body: Press Release International Law Enforcement Operation Targeting Opioid and Fentanyl Traffickers on the Dark Web Results in over 350 Arrests Worldwide and the Seizure of Drugs, Weapons, and over $234 Million Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Largest Takedown in JCODE’s History of Dark Web Narcotics Vendors Who Sold to Tens of Thousands of U.S. Residents Note: Relevant court documents can be found here . Today, the Department of Justice, through the Joint Criminal Opioid and Darknet Enforcement (JCODE) team, joined Europol to announce the results of Operation TorNado: a coordinated, multi‑agency and international law enforcement effort targeting criminal enterprises that use Dark Web markets to traffic fentanyl, opioids, and other illicit drugs. The operation, which was conducted across the United States, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, demonstrates the continued partnership between JCODE and Europol against the illegal sale of drugs and other illicit goods and services on the Dark Web. Operation TorNado represents the sixth — and most extensive — internationally coordinated action since JCODE was created in 2018 and builds on the success of last year’s Operation RapTor . This operation included actions against Dark Web vendors and buyers who were active on prominent Dark Web drug markets seized by law enforcement including: Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom, and Tor2Door. “Nothing will stop the Trump Administration from identifying and dismantling drug trafficking networks,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to our partnerships with state, federal, and international law enforcement through the Joint Criminal Opioid and Darknet Enforcement (JCODE) team, Operation TorNado crippled Dark Web market vendors and will bring alleged drug traffickers to justice. The Department of Justice will continue protecting the American people from lethal synthetic drugs and identifying bad actors around the globe who threaten American lives.” Following the takedown of multiple darknet marketplaces and vendor targets in the previous JCODE operation, U.S. and international law enforcement agencies obtained intelligence to identify Dark Web drug traffickers, resulting in a series of complementary, but separate, law enforcement investigations. Operation TorNado actions have resulted in the arrest of 354 Dark Web drug traffickers and fraudulent criminals who engaged in tens of thousands of sales of illicit goods and services across the United States, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand. This operation resulted in the seizure of over $234 million in both cash and virtual currencies; approximately 5.7 metric tons of illicit drugs worldwide, including fentanyl and other opioids, methamphetamine, heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, and MDMA, 38 pill presses; and 209 firearms. Dark Web vendor accounts were identified and attributed to real individuals selling illicit goods on Dark Web markets such as DrugHub, Archetyp, and others. By leveraging complementary partnerships and surging resources across the U.S. government and Europol, Operation TorNado significantly disrupted the online opioid trade and sends a strong message that criminals operating on the Dark Web are not beyond the reach of law enforcement. Operation TorNado led to 132 arrests in the United States, two in Australia, six in Austria, four in Czechia, one in Finland, 23 in France, 41 in Germany, 45 in Hungary, five in Ireland, 12 in the Netherlands, 13 in New Zealand, 11 in Slovenia, and 59 in the United Kingdom (UK). A number of investigations are still ongoing to identify the individuals behind Dark Web accounts. “Operation TorNado is the largest interagency takedown of Dark Web drug vendors and buyers to date, resulting in 354 arrests worldwide, including 132 in the United States,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Through the coordinated effort, this FBI and our partners collectively seized 5.7 metric tons of illicit drugs, including deadly fentanyl, as well as $234 million in cryptocurrency and cash. This FBI continues to accelerate our cyber capabilities including through our newly established Cyber Branch, evolving how we operate to meet the dynamic threat landscape presented by the Dark Web. The success of the Operation TorNado makes clear that criminals cannot hide behind technology or geography – no matter where you operate, justice will find you. Thank you to our JCODE and Homeland Security Task Force partners who continue to do elite work defending the homeland.” “Drug traffickers are exploiting the dark web to distribute fentanyl and other deadly drugs into American communities, profiting from addiction and overdose deaths,” said Administrator Terrance Cole of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). “Operation TorNado demonstrates the strength of JCODE and our international law enforcement partnerships. DEA, working as part of the Homeland Security Task Force through our field offices, played a significant role in identifying these criminals, exposing their trafficking networks, and disrupting their operations. Whether they operate on the streets or behind anonymous online accounts, DEA will use every available investigative tool to dismantle these organizations and bring those responsible to justice.” “Operation TorNado demonstrates the power of global partnership and underscores a vital truth: when the international law enforcement community stands united, borders offer no sanctuary to criminals,” said U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Chief Postal Inspector Gary Barksdale. “No matter where criminals attempt to hide, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service and our partners around the world will pursue them, dismantle their networks, and bring them to justice. Our commitment to protecting the public and holding these criminals accountable remains unwavering.” “The dark web is not a safe haven for criminals,” said Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). “This operation demonstrates what happens when law enforcement agencies around the world combine their intelligence, resources and expertise to dismantle criminal networks. With 354 arrests, more than five tons of drugs seized, and hundreds of millions of dollars in criminal assets taken out of circulation, we’ve sent a clear message: Criminals can operate in the shadows, but they can’t hide from justice.” “Criminal networks may operate across borders and in the shadows of the Dark Web, but they cannot operate without money,” said Chief Jarod Koopman of IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI). “IRS-CI is a global leader in financial crime investigations because our special agents have the expertise and international reach to follow the money, unravelling even the most complex schemes and exposing the people behind them. Operation TorNado demonstrates the power of combining financial intelligence with strong international law enforcement partnerships to disrupt illicit markets, seize criminal proceeds and hold traffickers accountable.” “The sale of illegal drugs through darknet marketplaces carries real and often tragic consequences for consumers and communities alike,” said Assistant Commissioner Justin Green of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Office of Criminal Investigations. “The FDA is steadfast in its commitment to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those who use these platforms to traffic in dangerous drugs at the expense of public health.” The extensive operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in dozens of federal prosecutions including: Stanislav Chernyshov, 30, a Russian national illegally residing in the United States, and his brother Vladislav Chernyshov, 35, a naturalized U.S. citizen, were arrested in Florida for allegedly operating Dark Web vendor “BarbaraWhite,” which sold counterfeit oxycodone M30 pills laced with highly potent nitazenes, synthetic opioids that can equal or surpass fentanyl’s potency. Lab analyses, covert purchases, and surveillance tied the brothers to a clandestine pill‑manufacturing and nationwide mailing operation allegedly responsible for over one thousand parcels shipped across 49 states, with multiple fatal and non-fatal overdoses identified among recipients of their products. They are charged with conspiracy to distribute Schedule I synthetic opioids in the Eastern District of Virginia. If convicted, they each face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. Alexander Green, 32, a U.S. citizen of Jacksonville, North Carolina, and formerly of Hazlet, New Jersey, was arrested in June for operating the STARLABS Cyber-Enabled Drug Trafficking Organization (DTO), an online vendor responsible for distributing a wide array of illicit narcotics - including fentanyl - on the Monero-only Dark Web market Drughub. Operating under the moniker “STARLABS,” Green’s DTO has been linked to two overdose deaths in the Southern District of Ohio. The June 2026 enforcement action resulted in the seizure of approximately 200 grams of methamphetamine and more than two kilograms of counterfeit pharmaceutical pills with fentanyl present. Green is charged in the Southern District of Ohio with conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances and distribution of controlled substances (fentanyl and methamphetamine). If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. Jonatan Gonzales, 35, a U.S. citizen of South Bakersfield, California, was arrested after he was identified as a Dark Web narcotics vendor “SpeedyPharma” who was shipping methamphetamine, as well as black tar heroin, cocaine, and K2 paper, to multiple addresses in western Pennsylvania, as well as to all other 49 states. Gonzales is charged with possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine in the Western District of Pennsylvania. U.S. law enforcement seized 48 lbs. of methamphetamine, 588 grams of cocaine, 386 grams of black tar heroin, 3.5 grams of fentanyl, 2.8 grams of carfentanil, and $40,565 in cash following a search of his residence. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of life in prison. Michael Morales, 25, of Bergenfield, New Jersey; Thomas A. Crisafulli, 27, of Bergenfield, Naudy Oviedo, 21, of Bronx, New York; Jayshawn Eyamazememba, 22, of Bronx, and Ethan Lara, 25, of Lodi, New Jersey, were arrested in New Jersey for their alleged roles in a New York/New Jersey distribution cell operating on behalf of a nationwide drug trafficking organization that distributed counterfeit Xanax, MDMA, ketamine, and other controlled substances through a nationwide mail-based distribution network. During the investigation, law enforcement executed search warrants at multiple locations and seized approximately 300 kilograms of counterfeit Xanax, MDMA, ketamine, and other controlled substances from a residence in Lodi, New Jersey, a storage unit in Lawrence Township, New Jersey, and other locations in Bergenfield and Englewood, New Jersey. The defendants were charged in Bergen County, New Jersey, with maintaining or operating a controlled dangerous substance production facility, manufacturing, distributing, or possessing with intent to distribute a controlled dangerous substance, and manufacturing, distributing, or possessing with intent to distribute marijuana or hashish. If convicted, they face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. The Bergen County Prosecutor's Office is handling the prosecution. Eric Turner, 30, of Lizella, Georgia, and Jose Smith, 29, of Valrico, Florida, both U.S. citizens, were arrested in June for operating a sophisticated Dark Web DTO primarily selling bulk quantities of heroin and fentanyl using the monikers Postmates and FuegoPacksXpress. Turner and Smith are charged with conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute heroin in the Middle District of Florida. U.S. law enforcement seized 4.5 kilograms of heroin, 22 grams of fentanyl, MDMA and alprazolam tablets and 25 firearms following a search of their residences. If convicted, they face a maximum penalty of life in prison. Operation TorNado was a collaborative initiative across JCODE members, including the Department of Justice; FBI; DEA; FDA Office of Criminal Investigations; HSI; IRS-CI; USPIS; Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF); Army Criminal Investigation Division (Army-CID); U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP); Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN); Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC); and Naval Criminal Investigative Service (NCIS). Local, state and other federal agencies also contributed to Operation TorNado investigations. The investigations leading to Operation TorNado were significantly aided by essential support and coordination by the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section; Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, the International Computer Hacking and Intellectual Property (ICHIP) prosecutor based in The Hague, Europol and its Dark Web team and international partners Eurojust, Australian Federal Police (AFP), Austria’s Criminal Intelligence Service with various Provincial Criminal Police Offices (Bundeskriminalamt und Landeskriminalämter); Czechia’s National Drug Headquarters - Criminal Police and Investigation Service (Národní protidrogová centrála SKPV PČR); General Directorate of Customs (Generální ředitelství cel); Finland’s Finnish Customs (Tulli); France’s National Gendarmerie (Gendarmerie Nationale); Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (Bundeskriminalamt); General Prosecutor’s Office in Frankfurt/Main, Central Office for Combating Cybercrime, Prosecutor’s Office in Cologne – Central Cybercrime Contact Point (Staatsanwaltschaft Köln, Zentral- und Ansprechstelle Cybercrime); Central Criminal Investigation in Oldenburg (Zentrale Kriminalinspektion Oldenburg); various police departments (Dienststellen der Länderpolizeien); German Customs Investigation (Zollfahndungsämter); Hungary’s National Bureau of Investigation and several police departments (Nemzeti Nyomozó Iroda); Ireland’s Garda National Cyber Crime Bureau (An Garda Síochána); Montenegro’s Police Directorate of Montenegro (Uprava policije Crne Gore); Netherlands Team High Tech Crime (National Investigations and Special Operations (NIS) and Post Interventie Team (PIT); National Intelligence, Expertise and Operational Support (NIEO); New Zealand’s Police (Ngā Pirihimana o Aotearoa); Slovenia’s Illicit Drugs Section in Criminal Police Directorate (Uprava kriminalistične policije), General Police Directorate in cooperation with the Criminal Police Directorate in Maribor (Policijska uprava Maribor) and the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC). Federal prosecutions are being conducted in more than 20 federal districts, including: the Central District of California, the Eastern District of California, the Northern District of California, the Southern District of California, the District of Colorado, the District of Columbia, the District of Connecticut, the Middle District of Florida, the Southern District of Florida, the Northern District of Georgia, the Middle District of Georgia, the Northern District of Illinois, the Northern District of Indiana, the Eastern District of Kentucky, the District of Maryland, the District of Massachusetts, the Western District of Michigan, the Eastern District of Missouri, the Western District of Missouri, the District of Nebraska, the District of New Jersey, the Southern District of New York, the Northern District of Ohio, the Southern District of Ohio, the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, the Western District of Pennsylvania, the District of Puerto Rico, the District of Rhode Island, the Eastern District of Texas, the Northern District of Texas, the Eastern District of Virginia, and the Western District of Wisconsin. JCODE is an FBI-led Department of Justice initiative to disrupt global drug‑trafficking networks and the digital infrastructure that enables them. Operation TorNado illustrates the investigative power of federal and international partnerships to combat the borderless nature of online criminal activity. The Justice Department is providing intellectual property and cybercrime technical assistance to foreign law enforcement, prosecutorial, and judicial partners in other countries through the ICHIP program. The Criminal Division’s ICHIP Program is jointly administered by the Criminal Division’s Office of Overseas Prosecutorial Development, Assistance and Training (OPDAT) and the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section through partnership between the U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs. An indictment and criminal complaint merely alleges that crimes have been committed. The defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Documents related to this announcement can be viewed here . title: Denver Man Sentenced To 180 Months In Federal Prison on Drug Distribution and Firearms Charges
body: Press Release Denver Man Sentenced To 180 Months In Federal Prison on Drug Distribution and Firearms Charges Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Colorado USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov DENVER – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado announces that Bryan Hjelmstad, 32, Denver, was sentenced to 180 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to possession with the intent to distribute greater than 500 grams of methamphetamine and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. According to the plea agreement, Hjelmstad was encountered by police at a Westminster hotel after employees complained that Hjelmstad was on drugs and running through the hotel.  Police later found over 700 grams of cocaine, 300 grams of methamphetamine, 30 grams of fentanyl, 19 grams of heroin, 237 grams of Xanax, 20 grams of MDMA, 13 grams of ketamine, three loaded firearms, multiple boxes of ammunition, and over $10,000 in cash in his hotel room. Six days later, police received a call from a Denver hotel after employees complained that the defendant was running through the halls with a shopping bag full of what appeared to be a large amount of narcotics. Hjelmstad fled before police arrived, but they located the shopping bag with 1.468 kilograms of methamphetamine hidden under a vehicle in Hjelmstad’s direction of flight.  Police also found over 40 grams of fentanyl pills, four additional firearms, and several hundred dollars in cash in his room. Hjelmstad was arrested shortly after fleeing the second hotel. “Mr. Hjelmstad was essentially daring anyone to hold him accountable, and now we have,” said United States Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “The community is safer now that this repeat offender who refused to stop committing very serious crimes will be off of our streets for a long time.” "A convicted felon on parole was caught with illegal firearms and narcotics, demonstrating a blatant disregard for the law and the safety of our community. Through a coordinated effort with the Westminster and Denver Police Departments, we leveraged federal authorities to remove a dangerous offender from our streets and send him to prison,” said FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski. “Let this serve as a clear message: Those who illegally possess firearms, traffic drugs, and contribute to violence in our communities will be identified, investigated, and prosecuted. We will continue to work tirelessly with our law enforcement partners to take guns, drugs, and violent offenders off the street and make our neighborhoods safer." United States District Judge Daniel D. Domenico presided over the sentencing. The FBI Denver Field Office, the Westminster Police Department, and the Denver Police Department handled the investigation. The Violent Crime Section of the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado handled the investigation. Case Number: 25-cr-129-DDD Contact USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov Updated November 12, 2026 Component USAO - Colorado

title: New York Doctor Charged in $6.8M Medicare Fraud Scheme
body: Press Release New York Doctor Charged in $6.8M Medicare Fraud Scheme Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs A federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida returned an indictment on Tuesday charging Dr. Edgard Salazar, 57, of Armonk, New York, with conspiring to bill Medicare for thousands of consultations that never occurred and millions of dollars of orthotic braces that Medicare patients did not want or need. According to court documents, telemedicine company TelevisitMD allegedly allowed Salazar to sign pre-filled prescriptions for Medicare beneficiaries who did not need the orthotic braces ordered in the prescriptions. Salazar did not examine or treat the beneficiaries and often did not speak to them at all. At times, when Salazar did speak to the beneficiaries, they told Salazar they did not want or need orthotic braces. Salazar signed prescriptions for them anyway. Salazar also billed Medicare for telemedicine consultations that he never performed. Salazar allegedly participated in submitting over $6.8 million in false and fraudulent claims to Medicare. Christopher Harwood owned and operated TelevisitMD. In March 2026, Harwood pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud and agreed to pay $17.9 million in restitution. Last month, Harwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in the conspiracy. Salazar is charged with conspiracy to commit health care fraud and five counts of health care fraud. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison on each count. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles of the FBI Miami Field Office; and Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) made the announcement. FBI and HHS-OIG investigated the case. Trial Attorney Owen Dunn of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section is prosecuting the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. title: Gootloader Malware Disrupted in International Cyber Operation
body: Press Release Gootloader Malware Disrupted in International Cyber Operation Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Colorado USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov DENVER — The Department of Justice today announced the successful removal of malware known as “Gootloader” from over 100 computer servers, including compromised WordPress sites, and the seizure of U.S. domain names used by criminals to deliver and control the Gootloader malware. Since 2018, Gootloader malware has infected at least 25,000 computers around the world. Gootloader malware has been used in ransomware attacks of at least 44 U.S. based victims which has resulted in approximately $28.8 million in loss. “With court authorization, the Department of Justice and FBI, along with our international partners, conducted an online operation that liberated over 100 servers from malicious software, denying ransomware criminals a platform,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “The Department of Justice has, once again, advanced President Trump’s Cyber Strategy by disrupting criminals’ cyber infrastructure.” “Cybercrime knows no borders and this case is an excellent example of international partnerships working to protect people around the world,” said U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly for the District of Colorado. “I am proud of the role we played in disrupting this botnet and thank our partners for their exceptional work to unearth this complex network.” “The Gootloader malware targeted victims on a global scale, including attacks on the U.S. Department of War and the Defense Industrial Base,” said Special Agent in Charge Kenneth DeChellis of the Department of War, formerly known as the Department of Defense, Office of Inspector General Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS), Cyber Field Office. “This announcement is a testament to the long-standing partnership and shared resolve between international law enforcement and private-sector organizations in pursuing cyber threats.” “Using a network of compromised websites, Gootloader malware infected thousands of computers worldwide, providing cybercriminals with access to deploy ransomware and cause millions of dollars in losses,” said Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI Cyber Branch. “Working alongside our partners, we disrupted the Gootloader botnet through coordinated technical operations, victim notifications, and remediation. Strong international and private-sector partnerships made this disruption possible, allowing us to protect victims from further harm and prevent future exploitation.” “Dismantling the Gootloader malware and botnet, which infected over 25,000 systems worldwide, demonstrates the power of unified, international law enforcement operations,” said Director L. Scott Moreland, Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division. “Alongside our global partners, Army CID is committed to taking the fight directly to cybercriminals. While disrupting these criminal networks stops ransomware attacks before they can take root, true cyber resilience relies on a combination of global law enforcement action and everyday personal vigilance.” According to warrants unsealed this week, Gootloader is malware that infects victim computers through a variety of means, often by tricking unsuspecting individuals into downloading it. Once infected, the compromised computers are added to a network of other compromised computers known as a botnet. The actors behind Gootloader used the botnet to infect other computers, then sell access to those later-infected computers to ransomware actors. In addition to the law enforcement seizures, the Shadowserver Foundation assisted by working with internet service providers and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) to identify infected systems, aid in notifying victims and assisting in remediation. Visitors to the seized domains will see the following seizure banner: These actions were conducted in coordination with Operation Endgame, a multinational law enforcement initiative targeting the dismantling of malware cybercriminal services. More information regarding Operation Endgame can be found at www.operation-endgame.com . The Gootloader investigation was led by DCIS, FBI’s Denver Field Office and the Army Criminal Investigative Division, working closely with Germany’s Bundeskriminalamt (BKA), the Netherlands National Police’s National High Tech Crime Unit, Canada’s Royal Canadian Mounted Police and Ottawa Police Service, Danish Police, Brigade de Lutte contre la cybercriminalité (Paris Cybercrime Unit), United Kindom’s National Crime Agency, the Australian Federal Police and Europol. ICHIP the Hague, Fraunhofer FKIE, Registrar of Last Resort (RoLR), OpenAI and Sharktech, Inc. also provided valuable technical assistance to the investigation. Senior Counsel Thomas Dougherty of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS) and Assistant U.S. Attorney Jasand Mock for the District of Colorado are prosecuting the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs also provided valuable assistance. CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 220 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $500 million in victim funds. The Justice Department is providing IP and cybercrime technical assistance to foreign law enforcement, prosecutorial, and judicial partners in other countries through the ICHIP program. The Criminal Division’s ICHIP Program is jointly administered by the Criminal Division’s Office of Overseas Prosecutorial Development, Assistance and Training (OPDAT) and CCIPS through partnership between the U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs. Contact USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov Updated November 12, 2026 Component USAO - Colorado

title: Wheeling Man Sentenced for Selling Drugs in Public Housing
body: Press Release Wheeling Man Sentenced for Selling Drugs in Public Housing Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of West Virginia WHEELING, WEST VIRGINIA – A Wheeling, West Virginia man was sentenced to a decade in prison for trafficking drugs from a public housing apartment, announced U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey. Roger Lee Williams, Jr., 32, was sentenced to 120 months in federal prison. Following a few sales of cocaine to a confidential informant, investigators executed a search warrant at the Booker T. Apartments where Williams lived. Officers seized cocaine and methamphetamine and found $3,040 from Williams. Williams has a criminal history that includes domestic violence, drug trafficking, larceny, obstruction, and fleeing. Assistant U.S. Attorney Clayton Reid prosecuted the case on behalf of the government. The Ohio Valley Drug Task Force, a HIDTA-funded initiative; the Drug Enforcement Administration; and the Ohio County Sheriff’s Office investigated. This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime, and repel the invasion of illegal immigration. U.S. District Judge John Preston Bailey presided. Updated November 12, 2026 Topics Operation Take Back America Drug Trafficking Component USAO - West Virginia, Northern

title: Federal jury convicts Lubbock man of methamphetamine distribution and firearm offenses
body: Press Release Federal jury convicts Lubbock man of methamphetamine distribution and firearm offenses Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Texas LUBBOCK, Texas — U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould announced that a 36-year-old Lubbock man was convicted on Nov. 10 of drug and gun charges following a multi-agency search warrant at his residence in January. Following a two-day trial presided over by U.S. District Judge James Wesley Hendrix, a federal jury took less than two hours to convict Jarrod Charles Gauna on all three counts charged in a May indictment. The convictions included conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, and possession of firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. ”The defendant chose to distribute dangerous drugs and carry a firearm in furtherance of that criminal activity. A jury held him accountable, and he now faces the possibility of spending the rest of his life in federal prison,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “Our office will never waver in its commitment to prosecuting those who profit by poisoning our communities, fueling addiction, and taking away the freedom and dignity of others. We will continue to use every lawful tool available to protect the public and deliver justice for the people of this district.” “Drug trafficking and its frequent companion, drug-related violence, place the safety of our communities at serious risk,” said DEA Dallas Special Agent in Charge Joseph B. Tucker. “This guilty verdict ensures Mr. Gauna is held accountable for his criminal actions, taking dangerous drugs and ready-to-use firearms off our streets before they can cause further harm and has undoubtedly saved lives.” According to evidence presented at trial, Lubbock Police Department and Drug Enforcement Administration narcotics agents became aware of Gauna’s residence in west Lubbock after it was involved in two different drug controlled purchases. During the first purchase in October 2025, Gauna’s codefendant, John Deleon, traveled to Gauna’s residence just prior to meeting with a confidential informant and delivering several ounces of methamphetamine. Deleon followed the same pattern before delivering additional methamphetamine to an informant in November 2025. Deleon pled guilty to methamphetamine distribution charges in August. On Jan. 15, narcotics agents executed a search warrant at Gauna’s residence.  Agents found approximately one-half ounce of methamphetamine along with several ounces of dimethyl sulfone, also known as MSM. The jury heard evidence that MSM is a substance that drug traffickers commonly use to “cut” methamphetamine to increase the quantity that can be sold. The jury also heard evidence that this same cutting agent was present in the methamphetamine that Deleon delivered to the informant during the controlled purchases. Agents also found four firearms in Gauna’s residence—three pistols and one over-under shotgun. All three pistols were loaded and readily accessible. One was located within inches of the drug evidence and the other two were in or near Gauna’s bedroom. A DEA drug trafficking expert explained the violence inherent in methamphetamine trafficking and how firearms such as these are used to protect drug dealers from being robbed. Gauna admitted to narcotics agents that the guns and drugs belonged to him. He also had several empty, unused baggies in his pocket. Witnesses testified that these baggies are commonly used to package methamphetamine for distribution. Gauna now faces up to life in federal prison. Because Gauna has a previous conviction for possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, he faces an enhanced minimum sentence of 25 years imprisonment following his second such conviction. Any sentence he receives for the drug charges must also run consecutively to the firearm charge. Gauna’s sentencing is scheduled for March 4, 2027. The Drug Enforcement Administration and Lubbock Police Department led this investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sean Long and Tyler Smotherman are prosecuting the case. Contact Public Affairs Division U.S. Attorney’s Office Northern District of Texas USATXN.Media@usdoj.gov Updated November 12, 2026 Topics Drug Trafficking Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Texas, Northern

title: Big Stone Gap Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Possession of a Firearm
body: Press Release Big Stone Gap Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Possession of a Firearm Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Virginia ABINGDON, Va. – A Big Stone Gap man, with a history of drug distribution, pled guilty last week to illegally possessing a firearm as a previously convicted felon. Jeremy Michael Boggs, 45, pled guilty last week to one count of possessing a firearm after having been convicted of a felony. Boggs has agreed to be sentenced to a term of imprisonment between eight and twelve years. According to court documents, on January 7, 2026, law enforcement received a call for trespassing at an apartment building in Wise, Virginia. Upon arriving at the scene, officers located Boggs in the laundry room of the apartment building and learned Boggs had an outstanding warrant for his arrest. As officers searched Boggs pursuant to his arrest on the outstanding warrant, an officer located an empty holster on Boggs’s belt. Wrapped inside a jacket Boggs had been wearing, officers found a loaded, Smith and Wesson revolver. In one of the jacket pockets, officers found a bag containing nine additional rounds of ammunition. Boggs was prohibited from possessing firearms due to at least four previous felony convictions in Virginia and Tennessee, including for drug distribution and aggravated assault. First Assistant United States Attorney Robert N. Tracci and Anthony Spotswood, Special Agent in Charge, ATF Washington Division, made the announcement made the announcement. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Wise Police Department, and Wise County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Corey Hall is prosecuting the case. Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Virginia, Western

title: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
body:
Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , the AWS SDKs , and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub . You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023 . The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/ , so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest
sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator . It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 , so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR , so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000 . curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java . For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
} When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline , and AWS CodeCommit , so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation. Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000 . curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java . For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
} When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline , and AWS CodeCommit , so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation. Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

title: Built on Googlebook: Play Henry Cavill’s video game to support Movember
body: Built on Googlebook: Play Henry Cavill’s video game to support Movember Nov 11, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link “Mustache Protocol” is live. See how the 16-bit adventure came together on Googlebook, and help us drive awareness for men’s health. Menaka Shroff (MK) Vice President, Marketing, Global Android Ecosystem Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We collaborated with Henry Cavill to create Mustache Protocol, a new 16-bit video game built entirely on Googlebook. You can play this retro-style game in your browser to support men’s health, as we will donate $11 to Movember for every play through November 30. Visit googlebook.com/henry to start your quest, watch the behind-the-scenes episodes, and contribute to this important cause. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Menaka Shroff, Vice President of Marketing, announces that Henry Cavill built a game called Mustache Protocol. You can play this retro-style game on your desktop or mobile device using simple arcade controls. We will donate 11 dollars to Movember for every game played until the end of November. Your participation supports awareness for men's mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We teamed up with Henry Cavill to create a retro video game called Mustache Protocol using our Googlebook tools. You can play this game in your browser to help us support Movember. For every game you play through November 30, we will donate $11 to men’s health causes, up to a total of $500,000. Visit our site to start playing, save the mustaches, and contribute to this important mission. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Henry Cavill teamed up with Google to build “Mustache Protocol,” a 16-bit video game, on his Googlebook. Over the past few weeks, we’ve watched Henry’s creative process unfold. In the first episode of our behind-the-scenes series, he designed a handlebar-mustachioed hero using Magic Pointer and Quick Access . In the second episode, he used Rambler to create superpowers and health boosts. Today, we’re sharing the final episode — and the game is officially ready for you to play. Watch the episode In the third episode of the series, Henry puts the finishing touches on his game. Every great game needs a theme song, and the finale shows how with a little help from Googlebook, Henry brought the game’s audio together. Let’s dive in: Continue On: Henry previewed a smooth, ’70s-style track on his Android phone, then used Continue On to move the music to his Googlebook desktop without interrupting his flow. Rambler and BandLab: After Henry plugged in a drum pad to add custom musical beats using BandLab and recorded sultry baritone vocals, Rambler turned his voice commands into clean prompts to drop the track and sound effects into the game. Antigravity: Using Antigravity , the next-gen agentic platform built into Googlebook, Henry stitched together the final visuals, level layouts, and interactive elements — the last steps in taking the game from an idea to a live, playable build. Play “Mustache Protocol” and support Movember “Mustache Protocol” is ready for you to play . The retro-style game sends players on an epic quest across three levels to stop a rogue CGI agent from erasing every mustache on the planet. It is, as Henry told us, "super serious." You can play directly in your web browser or on your desktop or mobile device using simple arcade controls to move, jump, and swing your mustache-comb sword. To make the game uniquely his, Henry packed each level with hilarious power-ups and Easter eggs. See if you can spot all of them. Henry steps up as the mustachioed hero to save the world’s mustaches this Movember. Keep an eye out for cameos from Henry's beloved dogs, Kal and Baggins. Power up with a “tank attack” and watch Henry celebrate with a dance. Power up with an “arm reload” to boost your attack power before a big fight. Quick tip for playing: an overview of keyboard controls. In honor of Movember , your gameplay supports men’s health. From November 11 to 30, for every game played, Google will donate $11 to Movember, up to $500,000. Every play helps drive awareness and funding for men’s mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer. So fire up your browser and help us save the world’s mustaches. Head to googlebook.com/henry to play “Mustache Protocol,” watch all three episodes, and join the movement. Check your inbox to confirm your subscription. You can also subscribe with a different email address . Your information will be used in accordance with Google's privacy policy. title: Get certified as a Google Cloud Professional Agentic Architect.
body: Get certified as a Google Cloud Professional Agentic Architect. Gary Eimerman Managing Director, Google GTM Learning Practice Lead Nov 11, 2026 Today we announced Google Cloud's new Professional Agentic Architect certification: an industry-recognized certification that proves you can deploy secure, enterprise-grade agents that automate multi-step and multi-app workflows. This hybrid certification has two parts: a proctored multiple-choice exam assessing foundational knowledge in agentic architecture, and Google Skills labs to evaluate real-world, hands-on practical experience. Over the past four months, Google Cloud has trained thousands of Google Cloud forward deployed engineers and Google Cloud partners on this advanced curriculum. This certification is now available for technical professionals like developers, cloud architects, and engineers who architect, build, and deploy agents on Google Cloud. Our research shows more than 80% of Google Cloud certified individuals say the credential opens doors to new career opportunities and accelerates their path to promotion. Furthermore, 82% of individuals say certifications from Google Cloud help them earn higher salaries 1 . Start your preparation at no cost today. Sign up for Gemini Agent Ready to claim 35 free monthly learning credits and gain access to our hands-on labs and agentic courses. Learn more on our Google Cloud blog .

title: Google Cloud leaders share what to expect in cybersecurity for 2027.
body: Google Cloud leaders share what to expect in cybersecurity for 2027. Nov 11, 2026 As enterprise software shifts from static applications to autonomous agents managing core operations, cybersecurity is facing a fundamental transformation. In our Security 2027 analysis, leaders from across Google, Google Cloud, and Mandiant break down the critical trends shaping the next era of defense. Key priorities for 2027 include : Protecting decision integrity: Ensuring every consequential autonomous action is secure and 100% explainable Moving "Beyond Zero": Never blindly trusting any AI tool, and having visibility into what they can access and what they are doing Winning with ground truth: Using multi-model AI ensembles to correlate internal context and remediate risks at machine speed before attackers can piece them together Watch the Security 2027 overview video below, and read the full executive perspective on the Google Cloud Blog .
